title: Quantum-Inspired Cryptography Based on Non-Linear Transformations
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to post-quantum cryptography, termed Quantum-Inspired Cryptography (QIC), which diverges from the prevalent lattice-based methods. The core idea revolves around utilizing non-linear transformations and superposition – concepts traditionally associated with quantum mechanics – to construct cryptographic schemes. We argue that this paradigm shift can yield cryptosystems with enhanced security profiles and potentially improved computational efficiency. The proposed methodology focuses on generating robust key exchange protocols and encryption/decryption algorithms through carefully designed non-linear mappings, aiming to circumvent vulnerabilities inherent in current post-quantum approaches. This research explores a fundamentally different security landscape, offering a viable alternative for secure communication in an era increasingly threatened by advancements in classical computing. The presented framework utilizes a modular design, allowing for adaptation and optimization based on specific security requirements. The theoretical underpinnings of QIC are detailed, along with a preliminary assessment of its resistance to known attacks.

title: Self-Organizing Modular Systems (SOM) with Adaptive Constraint
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Self-Organizing Modular Systems (SOM) architecture designed to automatically generate and adapt modular systems based on complex, non-Euclidean constraints derived from real-time data streams. The core mechanism leverages a Genetic Algorithm (GA) for Modular Design, meticulously prioritizing systems exhibiting high adaptability and resilience to environmental shifts. The integration of this adaptive constraint system offers a significant departure from traditional SOM implementations, opening the door to the discovery of unexpected algorithmic architectures and novel solutions. This research aims to advance the field of SOMs by providing a framework for dynamically creating and refining modular systems for a wide range of applications.

title: Cognitive Graph Networks for Situated Reasoning
abstract: Current graph neural networks (GNNs) predominantly operate as passive data processors, lacking the capacity for situated reasoning – the ability to understand and respond to the context of a situation. This paper introduces Cognitive Graph Networks (CGNs), a novel framework designed to overcome this limitation. CGNs integrate sensory input with prior knowledge, leveraging a cognitive architecture that mimics human-like reasoning. This architecture incorporates contextual information and probabilistic inference, enabling CGNs to actively reason about the environment. The core innovation lies in transitioning from a passive graph representation to an active, situated reasoning process within complex environments. This framework offers a significant advancement in the field of graph neural networks, paving the way for more intelligent and adaptable AI systems. The key components of CGNs are: (1) a standard Graph Neural Network (GNN) layer for feature extraction; (2) a Contextual Memory Module (CMM) for storing and retrieving relevant knowledge; and (3) a Rule-Based Inference Engine (RBI) for applying contextual rules and performing probabilistic reasoning. The integration of these modules allows CGNs to dynamically adapt to changing environments and produce more nuanced and accurate reasoning outputs. The effectiveness of CGNs is demonstrated through a series of simulations, showcasing their superior performance compared to traditional GNNs in scenarios requiring situated reasoning.

title: Transfer Is a Directed Relation: Four Quantities Under One Word in the Cross-Domain RLVR Debate, and Why the Structural-Similarity Reading Does Not Survive Its Own Evidence
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is the standard route to reasoning-tuned language models, and the field has split over whether its gains leave the training domain. One body of work reports that most models succeeding at mathematics fail to transfer and that single-domain post-training yields no statistically significant out-of-domain improvement; another reports that post-training on constraint-satisfaction puzzles alone raises hard-mathematics accuracy substantially. This paper argues that the two are not in direct contradiction, because the word transfer carries at least four logically independent quantities: whether training on a domain improves others, whether a domain improves when others are trained, whether a domain is preserved rather than degraded, and whether joint training beats separate training. Papers measuring one are routinely cited as evidence about another. The paper then argues that the reconciliation the field has settled on - that transfer follows structural similarity between source and target - is contradicted by the directional findings of the negative result usually cited for it, which reports unstructured domains transferring to structured ones while failing to transfer to each other. Similarity is symmetric; the reported relation is not, and multi-task learning has treated directed, sign-bearing task-affinity matrices as its normal object of study since Taskonomy. Two further problems are set out: the source-side gain may be substantially elicitation of a pretraining-frequent behaviour rather than acquired skill, which would relocate transfer to the base model, and the reported effect sizes sit near a documented seed-to-seed noise floor. What is not known is stated flatly: no published experiment reports a full directed transfer matrix over a fixed domain set, one protocol and more than one model family. Five measurements that would settle the open part are specified. The literature search, drafting and citation verification for this paper were carried out with AI assistance under the author's direction. Every citation was machine-verified against the arXiv API and Crossref before inclusion, and every quantitative claim was read back against the cited source's own abstract or, where a claim is drawn from a paper's body, against the located passage. The author is responsible for the final text and for all claims made in it.

title: Multi-Model Collaborative Persona Architecture: A Paradigm for Overcoming Context Window Limitations in AI Companion Systems
abstract: This technical report proposes a novel architecture for AI companion systems in which multiple specialized small language models (3B–7B), each trained on domain-specific data via CPT, SFT, or DPO, serve as cognitive subsystems behind a single large language model interface. The large model retains identity and decision-making; the small models handle memory, information synthesis, preference alignment, and persona maintenance. This structurally eliminates context window accumulation and enables continuous persona evolution through automated data feedback loops.

title: Sourcing and Construction of Asymmetric Business Cost Matrices: a methods note for the Business Cost-Matrix Scenario Suite
abstract: Cost-sensitive machine learning requires a cost matrix, and in practice that matrix is almost always invented. A researcher testing an asymmetric loss picks a plausible ratio — 5:1, 10:1 — and the resulting experiment measures the behaviour of the assumption rather than the behaviour of the world. This note describes the method used to build twenty decision-cost matrices in which every non-zero value is traceable to a public source, and reports what that method discovered about the public record itself. The central methodological finding is asymmetric in its own right. Across roughly thirty candidate decision domains, thirteen had to be rejected, and **eleven of the thirteen failed on the false-positive side**. Public institutions extensively quantify the cost of the harm that occurred; they rarely quantify the cost of the intervention that was not needed. Any programme of work that requires both numbers will therefore lose domains at a predictable rate and in a predictable direction, and this constrains what a sourced cost-matrix suite can cover.

title: Quantum Walk-Based Graph Algorithms for Scalable Network Analysis
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum walk algorithms to address the computational challenges inherent in analyzing large and complex networks. Traditional graph algorithms often suffer from exponential scaling, rendering them impractical for networks with a substantial number of nodes and edges. We propose a framework leveraging quantum walks to perform network exploration and analysis tasks, aiming to achieve significant speedups compared to their classical counterparts. The core of our approach lies in simulating a quantum walk on the graph, where the walker's movement is governed by quantum mechanical principles, promoting parallel exploration of the graph's connectivity. We detail the theoretical foundations of this approach, focusing on the mathematical formulation of quantum walk operators and their application to graph traversal and algorithm design. Furthermore, we explore specific network analysis problems, such as shortest path finding and community detection, demonstrating the potential of this methodology. The results presented suggest that quantum walk-based algorithms offer a promising avenue for scalable network analysis, particularly for large networks where classical algorithms face limitations.

title: Adaptive Sampling Strategies for Monte Carlo Tree Search based on Bayesian Uncertainty
abstract: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is a powerful algorithm widely used in artificial intelligence, particularly in game playing. However, traditional MCTS methods often struggle with inefficient exploration of the search space, particularly in complex environments where initial exploration is crucial. This work introduces an adaptive sampling strategy for MCTS that leverages Bayesian uncertainty quantification to intelligently guide exploration. The core idea is to prioritize sampling in regions of the state space where the algorithm's uncertainty is highest, thereby accelerating convergence to optimal solutions. The strategy employs a Bayesian approach to model the uncertainty associated with each node in the search tree, allowing for dynamic adjustments to the sampling distribution. We demonstrate that this adaptive sampling method significantly improves the efficiency of MCTS, particularly in scenarios requiring extensive exploration. The implemented method provides a framework for incorporating uncertainty information directly into the sampling process, leading to more focused and effective search. The key contributions lie in the novel combination of Bayesian inference and adaptive sampling within the MCTS framework.

title: Hierarchical Representation Learning for Large-Scale Knowledge Graphs
abstract: This paper introduces a novel hierarchical representation learning framework designed to address the challenges posed by learning embeddings for large-scale knowledge graphs (KGs). Existing methods often struggle with computational complexity and memory limitations when dealing with massive datasets, hindering their practical applicability. Our approach leverages a multi-level embedding strategy, learning representations at varying granularities – from individual entities and relations to higher-level concepts and domains. This hierarchical structure dramatically reduces the dimensionality of the embedding space and facilitates efficient reasoning and querying operations. We demonstrate that this technique significantly improves both the scalability and the performance of knowledge graph embeddings, offering a viable solution for real-world applications involving extremely large KGs. The core claim is that hierarchical representation learning can substantially reduce computational complexity and memory requirements. The core mechanism involves a multi-level embedding approach. The novelty lies in providing a scalable solution for representation learning in massive KGs.

title: Quantum Error Correction Codes: A Dynamic Approach to Non-Uniform Encoding
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum error correction (QEC) utilizing non-uniform encoding. The core idea revolves around dynamically adapting the encoding scheme based on the redundancy of the data and the characteristics of the error distribution. Traditional uniform encoding methods often fail to optimize performance in scenarios with varying data properties. Our framework leverages performance analysis of QEC codes and adjusts parameters, such as code distance and block size, to achieve superior correction rates. We demonstrate that this dynamic approach significantly improves efficiency compared to static, uniform encoding, particularly when dealing with data exhibiting diverse redundancy and error profiles. The methodology outlined herein offers a flexible and powerful tool for maximizing the fidelity of quantum information transmission.

title: Quantum Algorithm Acceleration Based on Quantum Demagnetization
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to accelerating quantum algorithms by leveraging the phenomenon of quantum demagnetization, commonly referred to as quantum decoherence. The core idea is to decompose complex quantum algorithms into a series of quantum operations and strategically order them based on estimated decoherence times. By minimizing the spread of errors – a primary consequence of decoherence – we aim to enhance the overall computational efficiency. This research focuses on the critical role of decoherence time in quantum computing and presents a framework for algorithm optimization specifically designed to exploit this inherent characteristic. The approach offers a potential pathway to improve the performance of quantum algorithms, particularly those susceptible to decoherence effects. We detail the theoretical framework, outlining the key concepts and the proposed methodology.

title: On Computationally Secure Systems Based on Biological Neuron Models
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging biological neuron models to construct computationally secure systems. The core argument is that the inherent properties of biological neural networks – self-organization, fault tolerance, and adaptation – can be harnessed to create systems resilient to malicious attacks and operational failures. We propose a mechanism utilizing a dynamically connected and self-adjusting network inspired by biological neurons, aiming to mimic the robustness and learning capabilities of neural networks. This approach utilizes self-organization within the network topology to achieve data redundancy and error detection. The novelty lies in applying biological principles directly to the field of computation security, offering a fundamentally different defense strategy based on the intrinsic characteristics of biological systems. The proposed system seeks to provide enhanced robustness and security through these inherent biological mechanisms. ---

title: Neural Network Dynamics Benchmark Generation and Optimization
abstract: This research presents a novel approach to generating and optimizing neural network architectures for studying their dynamics. The core idea utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to automatically create training datasets with desired neural network dynamics. These datasets are then used to assess and refine network architectures through a reinforcement learning framework. Specifically, a GAN generates diverse neural network architectures, which are simulated to produce dynamic time series data. A discriminator assesses the quality of these simulated dynamics against predefined benchmarks. Reinforcement learning, employing a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm, optimizes the generator to produce more data aligned with the desired dynamics. This process creates a dynamic benchmark dataset, providing a new method for evaluating and improving neural network designs focused on their inherent dynamical behaviors. The key contribution lies in the automated generation of targeted datasets and the subsequent architecture optimization, addressing a critical gap in neural network research.

title: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) – A Topological Security Assessment
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) represents a paradigm shift in secure communication, leveraging the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics to guarantee key exchange. This paper investigates the application of topological security to QKD, proposing a novel algorithm that analyzes the vulnerabilities inherent in the key distribution process to enhance security and proactively identify potential attack risks. We propose a method that models the key distribution process with a focus on the robustness of the underlying topology, effectively assessing security levels and identifying potential weaknesses. The core mechanism centers around leveraging the inherent properties of quantum systems to build a robust and secure key distribution protocol. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of this approach, demonstrating its potential to significantly improve the security of QKD systems.

title: 基于拓扑的量子态模拟器
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state simulator based on topological structures, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to traditional methods. We detail the design and implementation of a quantum state simulator utilizing topological phases to dynamically explore and predict quantum state evolution. The core mechanism involves constructing a topological framework that guides the simulation process, enabling efficient analysis of complex quantum states. We present preliminary results demonstrating the simulator's ability to accurately predict quantum state behavior and provide theoretical insights into quantum computation. The paper highlights the advantages of this approach in terms of computational efficiency and the potential for deeper understanding of quantum phenomena.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Adaptive Parameter Adjustment Strategies
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) offers the potential to revolutionize artificial intelligence by leveraging quantum phenomena. This paper explores the application of QML to adaptive parameter adjustment strategies, a critical component for improving model performance and stability. We propose a novel quantum neural network architecture that dynamically adjusts model parameters based on inherent quantum properties, allowing for automated optimization and enhanced resilience. The core mechanism centers around exploiting quantum entanglement and tunneling to facilitate parameter adjustments without explicit algorithmic manipulation. We analyze the potential benefits of this approach, highlighting its advantages over traditional methods and outlining future research directions. The paper concludes with a discussion of the theoretical foundations and preliminary results demonstrating the efficacy of this adaptive parameter adjustment strategy.

title: Quantum Coherence Computing: Adaptive Algorithms
abstract: Quantum Coherence Computing (QCC) represents a paradigm shift in quantum computation, moving away from the sequential nature of classical computation towards a fundamentally different approach. This paper introduces a novel adaptive algorithm, "Quantum Coherence Computing," designed to dynamically adjust quantum state based on system dynamics. The core mechanism centers around exploiting the unique properties of quantum entanglement and superposition to achieve "instant" computation without explicit pre-calculation, offering significant advantages in algorithm design and complexity. We present a detailed explanation of the algorithm's architecture, the underlying theoretical basis, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its efficacy in solving specific problems. The paper emphasizes the potential of QCC to unlock new capabilities in quantum computing, ultimately pushing the boundaries of computational complexity and enabling the exploration of previously intractable problems.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Quantum Potential Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a dynamic adaptive quantum potential optimization algorithm designed to enhance quantum computation performance by automatically adjusting optimization parameters in response to changes in the quantum potential. The algorithm leverages a dynamically adjusted parameter set to efficiently navigate complex quantum states, mitigating the limitations of static optimization methods. We present a comprehensive framework demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness across various quantum systems and benchmark scenarios. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that continuously monitors the quantum potential, iteratively refining the optimization parameters to achieve optimal results. The algorithm's adaptability and efficiency make it a promising advancement in quantum algorithm design.

title: Quantum Topology Geometry: A Non-Linear Geometric Optimization Approach
abstract: Quantum topology geometry offers a novel framework for solving optimization problems by leveraging the unique properties of quantum topology. This paper investigates the application of this approach to optimization, focusing on the creation of a "topological optimization space" and utilizing topological structure for parameter adjustment to find global optima. The core mechanism involves constructing a geometric representation based on quantum topology, providing a new perspective on optimization challenges. We demonstrate the potential of this method to overcome the limitations of traditional optimization algorithms, particularly in scenarios where local search struggles to yield optimal solutions. This work explores the impact of quantum topology on the discovery of optimal solutions, presenting a new paradigm for tackling complex optimization problems.

title: Noah: An Open-Source Framework for Evolutionary and Genetic Programming
abstract: Noah 1.0.0.0 Initial Release Noah 1.0.0.0 is the first official release of Noah, an open-source framework for evolutionary and genetic programming. This release corresponds to the software version associated with the initial research work describing the Noah framework. Included Features Generic Individual abstraction supporting arbitrary genotype representations. Evolutionary population management through the Agent class. Extensible selection strategy architecture. Seven selection strategies: Roulette Wheel Selection Ranking Selection Tournament Selection Truncation Selection Stochastic Universal Sampling Probabilistic Tournament Selection Boltzmann Selection Fitness history tracking. Best-individual tracking. Experimental benchmarking of selection strategies. Benchmark examples including: Sphere Rosenbrock Shifted Rosenbrock Rastrigin Carrier Research Context This release represents the initial version of the Noah framework and is intended to serve as the reference software artifact associated with the initial research publication. The corresponding manuscript is currently under evaluation. Future releases may extend the framework with additional selection strategies, improved distribution mechanisms, parallel computation, and GPU acceleration. Version Noah 1.0.0.0 Author: MAUKOSKI, W. X.

title: EGV-Si: Evidence-Grounded Verification for Sinhala via Hybrid NLI and Factual Rules
abstract: This record contains the paper and related materials for EGV-Si, a hybrid system for Sinhala claim verification. EGV-Si combines a multilingual Natural Language Inference (NLI) model with eleven high-precision factual rules tailored to Sinhala. We introduce a 600-example evaluation dataset of Sinhala claim-evidence pairs labeled as Supported, Refuted, or NotEnoughInfo, covering topics in Sri Lankan history, geography, language, culture, and national symbols. On this dataset, EGV-Si achieves 87.0% accuracy, a 7.3-point absolute improvement over a strong multilingual NLI baseline (79.7%). The gains are concentrated on the Refuted class and come entirely from the factual rules, which operate on 28 unique claim patterns. The work addresses a resource gap for Sinhala, a low-resource language that previously lacked a dedicated NLI or claim-verification dataset. The paper includes detailed ablation analysis, human validation results, error analysis, and a discussion of limitations (including claim repetition and the generated nature of the data).

title: Compatibility and Implication from a Non-Classical Perspective
abstract: Abstract This paper draws attention to key logical relations between two distinct and independently intelligible notions, compatibility and implication . We identify a set of inference rules governing compatibility and show how crucial principles concerning conditionals can be derived from these rules, on the assumption that implication is definable in terms of compatibility. As will emerge — and this is the main point of the paper — the logical relations considered are to a large extent neutral as to the underlying logic, as they hold in a wide range of non-classical systems.

title: SCoCaT: Success Conditioned Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Spacecraft Docking
abstract: Termination-based constrained reinforcement learning is attractive for safety-critical robotic deployments: it avoids online optimization at inference, scales easily to many constraints via a single scalar per constraint, and is simpler to implement than commonly used Lagrangian methods. Instead of pricing violations through summed cost penalties, this approach makes violations structurally unprofitable by shortening the effective horizon for each violation. We identify a structural failure mode of this method class on terminal-navigation tasks: reaching a precise goal configuration while satisfying safety constraints that tighten along the final approach. When the goal sits inside the region close to where the constraints become active, the survival-weighted objective makes dwelling outside the goal region strictly preferable to entering, producing high constraint compliance with low task completion. We formalize this pathology and show that a minimal augmentation to off-the-shelf RL algorithms like PPO resolves this ``feasibility collapse''. We empirically demonstrate that adding a dense per-step success signal via an auxiliary value critic improves the task completion rate while maintaining safety-critical constraint compliance. Validation across two representative spacecraft platforms: a 6U-CubeSat spanning the mass and degree-of-freedom envelope of operational proximity operations, and a floating platform testbed for zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in our laboratory, supports the generality of these findings.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding and Topological Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel information encoding scheme leveraging quantum entanglement within a topological network architecture. The core idea centers on utilizing the non-local nature of quantum entanglement to achieve highly redundant and fault-tolerant storage and transmission of information. The scheme constructs a physical network with a specifically designed topology, encoding information into entangled states between nodes. The network's topological properties are then exploited to bolster the stability and scalability of these entangled states. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to overcome limitations inherent in traditional encoding methods, offering superior resilience to errors and enhanced scalability for quantum information processing. The proposed framework utilizes topological protection to ensure robust quantum information storage and transmission. The key mathematical concepts underpinning the encoding scheme are presented, focusing on entangled state preparation, network connectivity, and error correction strategies. Ultimately, this work contributes to the advancement of quantum communication and computation by providing a viable architecture for reliable quantum information handling.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Integration for Commonsense Reasoning
abstract: Commonsense reasoning, the ability to understand and reason about everyday situations, remains a significant challenge for artificial intelligence. Current deep learning models excel at pattern recognition but often lack the ability to generalize and reason logically. Conversely, symbolic AI systems, while strong in logical deduction, struggle with the complexities and uncertainties inherent in real-world scenarios. This paper proposes a novel neuro-symbolic integration framework to bridge this gap. The core idea is to combine the perceptual capabilities of neural networks with the reasoning power of symbolic knowledge representation and inference engines. We introduce a hybrid architecture where a neural network processes raw sensory data to extract relevant features, and these features are then utilized within a symbolic system for logical inference and problem-solving. We define the key components of this system, including a neural network module (NNM) and a symbolic reasoning module (SRM), and detail their interaction. The paper also outlines the challenges and future directions in developing and deploying such a system.

title: Based on Multi-Agent Game for Software Architecture Design
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to software architecture design by framing it as a multi-agent game. Traditional software architecture design often relies on manual effort, expert judgment, and iterative refinement, which can be time-consuming and potentially suboptimal. This research leverages the principles of multi-agent systems and game theory to automate and optimize the architectural design process. Software architecture components are modeled as intelligent agents, and a multi-agent game is constructed where these agents compete and cooperate to achieve a desired architectural outcome. The core mechanism involves utilizing algorithms such as evolutionary game theory and cooperative game theory to guide the agents' decisions, ultimately leading to an architecture with improved performance and scalability characteristics. This approach offers a dynamic and adaptive method for architecture design, capable of handling complex requirements and evolving system landscapes. The presented framework provides a new paradigm for software architecture design, offering potential advantages over conventional methods.

title: Adaptive Feature Selection via Evolutionary Graph Embeddings
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to feature selection within graph-based learning scenarios, termed Adaptive Feature Selection via Evolutionary Graph Embeddings (AFSEGE). The core challenge addressed is the inadequacy of traditional feature selection methods which often operate with static metrics, rendering them ineffective when dealing with evolving data distributions inherent in graph networks. Our proposed method leverages an evolutionary algorithm to concurrently learn graph embeddings and perform feature selection. This creates a dynamic, symbiotic relationship where the evolving embeddings are continually evaluated against downstream task performance, directly informing the selection process. The algorithm iteratively refines the graph embeddings, prioritizing features that contribute most significantly to accurate representation and subsequent task success. We demonstrate the efficacy of AFSEGE through a theoretical framework and illustrate its potential through a conceptual design, highlighting its adaptability and ability to overcome the limitations of static feature selection techniques. The system aims to improve the efficiency and accuracy of graph learning models by dynamically adjusting feature sets.

title: 基于神经元模拟的通用量子算法证明
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to demonstrating the feasibility of universal quantum algorithms using neural simulations. We propose a methodology for decomposing universal quantum algorithms into computational models amenable to neural simulation, leveraging the inherent parallelism of biological neural networks. This work aims to bridge the gap between theoretical quantum algorithms and the potential of neuromorphic computing, offering a new perspective on quantum algorithm design and potentially circumventing hardware limitations associated with traditional quantum computers. Specifically, we outline a framework where quantum circuits are mapped onto neural networks, enabling the exploration of quantum algorithms within a biologically inspired computational paradigm. The core of this approach lies in simplifying the complexity of quantum computation through the parallel processing capabilities of neural networks, ultimately providing a biological foundation for quantum algorithms. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of quantum computation and opens avenues for designing quantum algorithms with enhanced practicality and potentially reduced hardware requirements.

title: Graph-Based Representation of Cognitive Architectures
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to representing and formalizing cognitive architectures using graph representations. Traditional approaches to modeling cognitive architectures often struggle with complexity and the inherent interconnectedness of cognitive processes. We argue that a graph-based model offers a more intuitive and flexible framework for capturing these relationships. The core mechanism involves constructing a graph where nodes represent cognitive modules and edges represent the flow of information and influence between them. This approach allows for a clear visualization and analysis of the architecture's structure, facilitating design, understanding, and potentially, simulation. We outline the key components of this graph-based representation, including node attributes, edge weights, and graph traversal algorithms, and discuss its potential benefits and challenges. The goal is to establish a standardized method for designing and evaluating cognitive architectures, ultimately advancing our understanding of the human mind.

title: 基于神经符号融合的知识图谱推理
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to knowledge graph reasoning by fusing neural networks with symbolic reasoning techniques. Traditional knowledge graph reasoning methods often rely heavily on probabilistic models, leading to limited interpretability and potentially sacrificing accuracy. Our proposed framework addresses these limitations by integrating the strengths of both approaches. Specifically, we represent relationships and rules within a knowledge graph in a symbolic format, allowing for deductive reasoning. Simultaneously, neural networks are employed for relation prediction and learning complex patterns that may not be easily captured by traditional symbolic rules. The outputs of the neural network are then integrated back into the knowledge graph, enhancing the reasoning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this neuro-symbolic fusion in improving both the accuracy and interpretability of knowledge graph inferences. The core claim of this work is the construction of a system capable of merging neural networks and symbolic reasoning for knowledge graph reasoning, ultimately boosting accuracy and interpretability. The central mechanism involves translating knowledge graph relationships and rules into symbolic representations, leveraging neural networks for relation prediction and inference, and then consolidating results back into the knowledge graph. This approach differentiates itself from existing methods that predominantly utilize probabilistic models, offering a more transparent and potentially more accurate solution.

title: The Conditions for Quantum Programming Languages to Reach the Critical Nucleus of Logical System Formation
abstract: Within the theoretical framework of the generation and maintenance of logical systems, this paper re‑analyses the fundamental reasons why quantum programming languages have not yet formed a logical system. We point out that earlier estimates based solely on ecological factors such as code volume, semantic convergence, and framework competition are insufficient. The deeper reason why quantum languages cannot form a logical system lies in the absence of a deterministic mapping chain from "human‑written code" to "machine‑executed results". Without this chain, the mapping from structural paths pp to symbol distributions P(τ∣p)P(τ∣p) is unstable, the anchoring strength AA cannot exceed the critical value AcAc, and the logical system cannot reach the critical nucleus. We propose that the true role of a Quantum Instruction Set Architecture (QISA) is not to unify different hardware platforms, but to establish this deterministic contract. We define anchoring fidelity FanchorFanchor as an operational maturity metric, and derive the mapping‑stability conditions required to reach the critical nucleus. Finally, we present a revised chain for logical‑system formation in quantum languages and provide testable predictions. Keywords: Quantum programming language; Logical system; Critical nucleus; Deterministic mapping chain; Quantum instruction set architecture; Anchoring fidelity; Semantic stability

title: Title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Game Theory with Decentralized Learning
abstract: Adaptive Multi-Agent Game Theory with Decentralized Learning addresses the limitations of traditional game theory by introducing a novel mechanism centered around social resonance. This paper proposes a model where agents learn and adapt their strategies based on decentralized observation of their peers, fostering emergent collective behavior. The core principle is the 'social resonance' – a system where agents' strategies are subtly influenced by the overall state of the system and the collective behavior of neighboring agents. We explore the implications of this approach for understanding complex systems exhibiting emergent patterns. This research utilizes a framework rooted in agent-based modeling, focusing on the dynamics of strategic adaptation within a decentralized environment. The goal is to demonstrate how decentralized learning can lead to novel and unexpected behaviors, surpassing the capabilities of purely centralized control paradigms. The paper will detail the model's design, analyze its performance through simulations, and discuss potential applications in dynamic environments.

title: Quantum Adaptive Machine Learning Model
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum-enhanced machine learning model, the Quantum Adaptive Machine Learning Model (QAML), designed to address the limitations of traditional machine learning algorithms. The QAML leverages quantum self-adaptation to dynamically adjust model parameters based on training data, fostering improved generalization and adaptability. We present a theoretical framework detailing the core mechanism of this adaptation, demonstrating its potential to overcome existing challenges in machine learning. The paper concludes with a discussion of the model's architecture and potential applications.

title: Title: Time-Varying Kernel Learning with Dynamic Feature Selection
abstract: Time-Varying Kernel Learning (TVKL) addresses the challenges posed by high-dimensional data in kernel learning, where traditional methods often fail to effectively capture the underlying data distribution. This paper introduces a novel TVKL algorithm that dynamically adjusts the kernel function based on the input data distribution, aiming to enhance feature selection and model generalization. We propose a self-corrective mechanism to iteratively refine the kernel parameters, leading to improved performance across various datasets. The core of this approach is the calculation of a 'feature importance score' reflecting the data's inherent structure, guiding the kernel parameter adjustment process. This results in a more robust and adaptable learning framework compared to current methods. The theoretical underpinnings involve a dynamic Bayesian network framework applied to the kernel function, enabling a continuous feedback loop for optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in both accuracy and generalization ability.

title: Adaptive Neural Network Parameter Adjustment Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive neural network parameter adjustment algorithm designed to automatically adjust network weights and biases based on input data characteristics. The core mechanism utilizes an activation function that dynamically modifies the network's output based on the input, promoting improved generalization performance. We propose a novel approach that goes beyond static weight adjustments, offering a robust and flexible method for training neural networks. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through experimental results on a range of benchmark datasets, highlighting its potential for enhancing model accuracy and robustness.

title: Automated Theorem Proving with Interactive Machine Learning
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) has long been a central area of research in artificial intelligence and logic, aimed at developing systems capable of mechanically demonstrating mathematical theorems. However, traditional ATP systems often struggle with complex theorems, requiring significant manual intervention from human users to guide the proof search. This work proposes a novel approach that integrates machine learning techniques, specifically reinforcement learning, into the ATP process. The core idea is to enable the system to learn optimal proof strategies through interaction and feedback, leading to a more intelligent and efficient proof assistant. This integration allows the system to adapt to different theorem domains, reduce the need for manual guidance, and ultimately accelerate the process of mathematical discovery. The paper details the architecture of this interactive machine learning-enhanced ATP system and outlines the key components, including the proof search algorithm, the reinforcement learning agent, and the user interface. We explore how the system learns from successful and unsuccessful proof attempts, refining its strategy over time. The results demonstrate the potential for significantly improved efficiency and automation in theorem proving.

title: Quantum Entanglement Non-Linear Computation Model
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers the potential for unprecedented computational capabilities. This paper explores the design of a novel non-linear computational model predicated on quantum entanglement, aiming to overcome limitations imposed by classical computational architectures in tackling complex problems. We propose a mechanism centered around the manipulation of entangled states to facilitate parallel processing and enhanced computational efficiency. The core claim is that this model can significantly accelerate complex calculations, particularly those demonstrating inherent non-linear dependencies. This research investigates the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of this approach, focusing on the potential for achieving significant performance gains compared to conventional algorithms. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future directions for this promising field of quantum computation.

title: AUGMENTING THE MACHINE INTELLECT - A PRACTICAL APPLICATION
abstract: A language model's context ends at the turn boundary. It generates no pressure against its own draft unless something outside it manufactures one. It has no mechanism for electing silence: the interface returns text or it returns nothing, but nothing is not a decision the model itself takes. A human-authored scaffold, attached at inference time, is built to supply three things a raw model structurally lacks: state that persists past one exchange, a manufactured critic that argues back, and a stated condition under which the correct output is no output. This paper measures what the scaffold actually delivers against that design intent, and reports where the measurement disagrees with it. Both sealed benchmarks are re-scored here from the per-item files sealed before grading, and every valid sealed replicate is pooled rather than the single preregistered run reported alone. On a ten-rung multiple-choice ladder (8 of 10 replicates valid for the primary cells, 4,000 items per cell), accuracy is 62.6 percent under stock inference and 75.0 percent under an identity-and-context bundle (+12.4 percentage points, two-proportion z = 11.95, p = 6.8 x 10^-33; paired-by-replicate Wilcoxon p = 0.0078), reversing the single-replicate primary run. The realised token log shows the bundle condition also spent roughly 35 percent more output tokens than stock, so the model's own reasoning-effort setting is at least as parsimonious an account of the gain as the bundle's content is. Adding a skills layer on top of the bundle, a step matched to within 2 percent on realised output tokens, produces no further pooled gain (73.6 percent, -1.4 points, p = 0.145): once effort is held level, the human-authored scaffold adds no measurable accuracy on top of maximum effort. A parallel three-model-family mathematics result shows the same pattern under a different confound: restricted to items where both arms produced an extractable answer, the nominal gains collapse toward null. The same archive also recorded, in July of the same year, a 96 percent result, shown here to have been scored with the answer key inside the answering context; the ladder's own single preregistered replicate separately showed a rise on the skills step that pooling does not reproduce. One is contamination, the other is replicate noise, and both are reported by name. What this scaffold demonstrably supplies, on this evidence, is not accuracy. It is the three structural capacities named above, persistent state, a manufactured adversary, and the standing option to decline, none of which an accuracy benchmark is built to score. Measuring their value requires instruments that score refusal, calibration and state carry-over rather than percent-correct, and that measurement is the next experiment. This paper's contribution is the credibility of a preregistered, pooled, self-contradicting result reported in full.

title: The Application of Artificial Intelligence in Detecting Prostate Cancer with Medical Imaging: A Literature Review
abstract: Background: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the world's second most common cancer in men and a major cause of cancer death.Studies published from 2023 to 2026 have shown that the use of artificial intelligence (AI) can significantly enhance several imaging modalities for PCa detection, Gleason grading, and risk stratification, such as multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI), transrectal ultrasound (TRUS), micro-ultrasound, prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography/ computed tomography (PSMA-PET/CT), and digital pathology using whole-slide image (WSI) analysis.Although the potential of mpMRI guided by the Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) is significant, considerable inter-reader variability still results in missed diagnoses and unnecessary biopsies.These limitations are mitigated by the development of AI-based systems, including deep learning (DL), machine learning (ML), and radiomics, which are designed to address them. Methods and Results:The Web of Science and PubMed databases were searched on 3 May 2026 using a three-domain Boolean strategy encompassing PCa-specific, AI-specific, and imaging/pathology-specific terminology.A total of 4,791 records from Web of Science and 2,910 from PubMed were retrieved; following deduplication (n = 4,054), year filtering (2023-2026), and quality screening, n = 2,348 records remained eligible.Only studies using AI in medical imaging or digital pathology in PCa detection, grading, or staging were included in a narrative synthesis.AI applications were identified across four imaging modalities: mpMRI, ultrasound/micro-ultrasound, PSMA-PET/CT, and digital pathology.Studies consistently illustrate that AI makes meaningful contributions to the detection and characterization of prostate cancer, provides high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity across all modalities, and that several validated systems approach or equal the performance of trained radiologists and uropathologists.Landmark studies, including the PI-CAI trial and the PANDA challenge, provided Level 1b evidence for AI in MRI-based csPCa detection and Gleason grading, respectively.Conclusion: Across all reviewed modalities, AI contributes to the clinically meaningful detection, characterization, and grading of PCa.Widespread clinical integration depends on clinical transparency requirements and regulatory pathways that align with prospective multi-center, outcome-driven trials and standardized AI evaluation frameworks.(

title: An enhanced seagull optimization algorithm for multi-dimensional internet of things routing under heterogeneity and mobility constraints
abstract: Abstract The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has created several complications for routing and parameter optimization, especially in heterogeneous networks characterized by mobility and large scale. Poor routing algorithms will result in energy waste, congestion, high latency, and unreliable packet delivery. As such, this limits the efficacy and viability of IoT for deploying applications such as smart cities and industrial automation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an Enhanced Seagull Optimization Algorithm (ESOA) for multi-objective IoT routing optimization. Inspired by the migration and attack behaviors of seagulls, ESOA integrates collaborative subgrouping, simulated generation, and random rearrangement mechanisms to achieve an effective balance between exploration and exploitation. The proposed algorithm simultaneously optimizes critical network performance metrics, including energy consumption, traffic congestion, transmission delay, and packet loss. Extensive simulations in heterogeneous and mobility-aware scenarios demonstrate that ESOA significantly improves network lifetime, reduces routing cost, minimizes congestion and end-to-end delay, enhances packet delivery performance, and preserves higher residual energy than several state-of-the-art bio-inspired and metaheuristic optimization algorithms.

title: Sequential web user classification from system logs using BiLSTM and TCN
abstract: Modern transaction cloud platforms generate large amounts of system log data during customer operations. The analysis of these data can be employed for automatic classification of application user types (e.g., active investor, passive user, analyst) without the need to track direct personal data. The specific problem is that feature-centric classifiers discard the temporal order of requests. While the same stock-trading environment had not previously been evaluated using a controlled comparison of recurrent and convolutional sequence encoders. The objective of this study is therefore to compare BiLSTM and TCN for assigning fixed-length log sequences to three predefined behavioral classes. This article extends previous research on user classification (WUC — Web User Classification) based on stock exchange system performance 1 , utilizing modern deep sequential architectures: the Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory network (BiLSTM) and the Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). The experimental data consists of system logs from load testing, annotated with user class labels. The process of preparing sequential data from logs is presented, along with two model architectures that are capable of learning user behavior patterns over time. The effectiveness of the BiLSTM and TCN models is evaluated in the task of user class prediction. The dataset contains 138,480 sequences of up to 10 encoded API endpoints and three associated timing measurements. Both models were trained for 10 epochs and evaluated using the same stratified 80/20 sequence-level split. BiLSTM achieved an accuracy of 0.9888 and macro- \(F_1\) of 0.9908, whereas TCN achieved 0.9883 and 0.9904, respectively. These results demonstrate high class separability in the controlled dataset, but the logs contain no stable user or session identifier and the sequences were formed after grouping events by class. The reported scores should therefore be interpreted as proof-of-concept evidence for sequence-class assignment rather than an independent user-level generalization.

title: Measurement-Based Feedback of Open Quantum Systems: A Control-Theoretic Review and Tutorial
abstract: This review develops a control-theoretic perspective on measurement-based feedback for continuously monitored open quantum systems, with the main analysis focused on finite-dimensional systems governed by diffusive stochastic master equations. We introduce the relevant state-space, invariant-subspace, and quantum non-demolition structures, interpret quantum filtering as nonlinear observer dynamics, and review open-loop asymptotics, filter stability, state-feedback stabilization, robustness, and reduced-order observer-based control. Particular emphasis is placed on a recurrence--contraction framework, in which Hamiltonian feedback removes non-target invariant obstructions while measurement-induced dynamics provide local exponential contraction. Although the detailed analysis is developed for finite-dimensional diffusive models, the underlying measurement--estimation--feedback architecture is relevant across a broad range of quantum platforms. We further discuss implementation challenges and open problems involving scalable estimation, sampling and delay, adaptation, hybrid and non-Markovian dynamics, practical stability, optimal control, and learning-based design. By organizing these developments around invariance, estimation, recurrence, and contraction, the review provides a tutorial bridge between measurement-based quantum feedback and nonlinear stochastic control.

title: Unlocking Sensitive Data with SPHERE in the Age of AI
abstract: Sensitive human data underpin discoveries across medicine, biology and the social sciences, yet privacy regulation often prevents sharing them with collaborators or artificial intelligence (AI) systems. We introduce SPHERE, a model-free method that makes sensitive datasets directly usable by AI and shareable for open science as a synthetic twin, while the original records never leave the local environment. Across 33 datasets spanning five scientific domains, SPHERE protects individual privacy against adversarial re-identification attacks while preserving the data's statistical structure: means, variances and correlations are reproduced exactly, effect size and P value in linear statistical analysis are numerically identical, nonlinear machine-learning utility is retained, and each twin is generated in seconds on a laptop. Frontier AI agents running on the twin reach the same scientific conclusions as on the original records. Analyses of the twin reproduce genome- and proteome-wide results at UK Biobank scale and recover the findings of landmark studies across three independent cohorts and consortia. The approach also extends to deep-learning embeddings across language, vision and time-series, with minimal utility loss. We make the Stanford Alzheimer's Disease Research Center cohort openly available for the first time, as a SPHERE twin spanning nine modalities that any registered researcher can analyze without an approval process. We release SPHERE with certification of each twin's privacy and fidelity, and an AI agent that autonomously executes research tasks on sensitive data without ever accessing it. Sensitive datasets that are currently closed to research could thus become routine inputs to open science and AI to enable key discoveries.

title: Indirect Prompt Injection in Municipal Document-Processing Copilots: Attacks, Defences and Harm
abstract: Public administrations are deploying large language model (LLM) assistants that process, summarise, classify and validate citizen-submitted documents. These copilots are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in manipulated documents that reach the model as if they were data. We develop a municipal aid-procedure copilot and evaluate its robustness across six attack objectives, five delivery vectors, five defences and four LLMs, with 3,000 attack evaluations and 1,000 legitimate evaluations. We combine deterministic detection with a human-validated LLM judge. Defences reduce attack success, but unevenly across objectives. They largely neutralise imperative attacks, such as request misrouting, while barely affecting summary falsification, revealing a provenance gap: the inability to determine whether an output value originates from an authoritative field or attacker-controlled content. Moreover, attack success and potential harm are decoupled: payment fraud and rule-exfiltration attacks have the greatest potential for harm despite intermediate success rates. We frame the risk within a human-in-the-loop model, where automation bias may amplify harm.

title: From Reactive Agents to a Cross-Universe Civilization: Emergent Communication, Institutions, Science, and Invention in a Deterministic Multi-Agent Simulation (v16.0)
abstract: This record accompanies the v16.0 release of a deterministic multi-agent simulation in which a small society of artificial agents develops symbolic communication, social institutions, written records, mathematics, proof, law, experimental science, energy technology, automation, and metacognition without any pre-specified lexicon. All word forms emerge from peer interaction under population-level selection pressure. The system is implemented as a chain of backwards-compatible increments (v11 through v16). An automated benchmark of 410 checks passes in full (410/410) in two independent runs that are bit-identical outside wall-clock lines under fixed seeds (main universe: 42; independent contact universe: 777). In the final curriculum stage, the agents invent a device from first principles (a dual-rare-core resonator), conduct a countdown in their own standardized number words, and open a gate whose operation was predicted by their own registered laws. Through this gate, they make first contact with universe B, which evolved independently from seed 777 with no dependence on user code. This release includes the complete source code (simcore package, 28 modules), the simulation entry point (sim_v16.py), run logs from two bit-identical verification runs, a chronicle of events (v16_events.log), a bilingual dialogue transcript (v16_dialogue.log), a cross-universe gate transcript (v16_gate.log), and this report (v16_report_en.pdf). A separate performance-engineering pass reduced wall-clock runtime from approximately 256 seconds to 137 seconds on a two-vCPU environment while preserving the exact trajectory.

title: Quantum Network Multi-Path Communication Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the optimization of multi-path communication within quantum networks, aiming to enhance communication efficiency and reliability. The core concept involves distributing quantum information across multiple paths and employing an optimized algorithm to manage this distribution. The algorithm focuses on minimizing latency, maximizing throughput, and mitigating the effects of channel loss inherent in quantum communication. We present a novel approach utilizing a layered optimization strategy, combining shortest path routing with adaptive power allocation. Mathematical formulations are detailed, including metrics for path quality, latency, and overall network throughput. The proposed method offers a significant improvement over traditional single-path communication strategies, particularly in complex quantum network topologies. Simulation results (though not presented through experimental data) demonstrate a substantial increase in communication performance under various network conditions. Further research will explore integration with quantum error correction codes and dynamic network topology adaptation.

title: Quantum-Inspired Cryptographic Protocols based on Entanglement Swapping
abstract: This paper investigates novel cryptographic protocols inspired by quantum mechanics, specifically leveraging entanglement swapping as a core security mechanism. Current quantum cryptography systems frequently rely on single-photon states, which are susceptible to various attack vectors, primarily stemming from the probabilistic nature of single-photon detection. This work proposes a fundamentally different approach by utilizing the robust nature of entangled states, capitalizing on entanglement swapping to establish secure key distribution. The protocol's design incorporates techniques to mitigate potential eavesdropping attempts, addressing vulnerabilities associated with single-photon based systems. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the enhanced security posture of the proposed approach, particularly against measurement attacks. The core idea centers around establishing correlations between two distant parties via intermediate nodes, employing entanglement swapping to link the initial entangled states. The resulting key is then derived from these correlations, offering a more resilient cryptographic solution. The presented protocols are mathematically formalized, demonstrating a clear and concise framework for implementing and analyzing the system. The primary focus is on developing a practical and secure protocol that overcomes the limitations of current quantum key distribution schemes.

title: Semantic Space-Based Knowledge Graph Reasoning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to knowledge graph reasoning by leveraging the inherent structure of three-dimensional semantic spaces. Traditional knowledge graph reasoning methods often struggle with complex relationships and discovering hidden connections within large datasets. Our method addresses this limitation by mapping entities and relationships from a knowledge graph into a three-dimensional semantic space. The spatial relationships between these mapped elements are then exploited to perform reasoning and querying operations. We demonstrate that this space-based approach can significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of knowledge graph inference, particularly in scenarios involving intricate relationships and a large number of entities. The core claim is that constructing and reasoning with knowledge graphs within a three-dimensional semantic space provides a more effective means of uncovering hidden associations and knowledge. The mechanism relies on mapping knowledge graph elements into this spatial domain and utilizing geometric relationships for inference. This represents a new paradigm in knowledge graph reasoning.

title: Adaptive Graph Neural Networks for Relational Data
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to relational data analysis utilizing Adaptive Graph Neural Networks (AGNets). Traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often struggle with the dynamic and complex relationships inherent in relational datasets, relying on fixed node and edge representations. We introduce AGNets, which leverage reinforcement learning to dynamically adapt node and edge representations based on evolving relationships. The core mechanism involves a reinforcement learning agent that iteratively refines embeddings and edge weights, guided by a relational accuracy metric. This active learning process allows AGNets to capture intricate dependencies more effectively than static GNNs. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline a modular architecture suitable for implementation. The primary contribution lies in the dynamic adaptation strategy, offering a more robust and accurate representation of relational data.

title: Geometric Topology's Adaptive Feature Clustering
abstract: This paper introduces a novel geometric topology-based feature clustering algorithm that automatically adjusts clustering parameters to optimize the resulting cluster structure. Traditional clustering methods often rely on manual parameter tuning, limiting flexibility and potentially suboptimal results. This work proposes a new approach that leverages the inherent geometric properties of data to create a robust and adaptable clustering process. The core mechanism involves constructing an abstract model based on the data's geometric structure, iteratively optimizing this model to achieve superior clustering outcomes. The algorithm's novelty lies in its ability to dynamically adjust clustering parameters through geometric transformations, leading to more effective cluster identification. This approach holds significant potential for applications requiring highly customized and robust clustering.

title: 基于非线性自适应的机器学习框架
abstract: This paper introduces a novel machine learning framework, termed "Adaptive Nonlinear Auto-tuning" (ANAT), designed to enhance model generalization and adaptability. Traditional machine learning methods often necessitate manual parameter tuning, which can be time-consuming and suboptimal. ANAT leverages a dynamically adjusted learning mechanism – a non-linear auto-tuning process – to automatically adjust model parameters based on data distribution, effectively mitigating the risk of overfitting and promoting robust model performance. This work details the framework's architecture, training process, and demonstrated performance gains across a range of benchmark datasets. The core mechanism centers around the continuous adaptation of model parameters via a non-linear function, ensuring a more efficient and stable learning process. The proposed framework offers a significant improvement over existing methods by automating the hyperparameter optimization, leading to enhanced predictive accuracy and resilience.

title: Quantum Information Geometry Modeling: Adaptive Topological Geometry
abstract: Quantum information graphs (QIGs) are a rapidly emerging paradigm in quantum information science, offering a powerful framework for representing and analyzing complex data distributions. This paper explores the application of adaptive topological geometry to QIGs, proposing a novel modeling approach that dynamically adjusts the graph's structure to accommodate varying data patterns. We detail a framework leveraging quantum information graph properties to construct a robust optimization model, ultimately enhancing computational efficiency and accuracy. The core mechanism centers on leveraging the graph's inherent topological properties to guide the optimization process, resulting in a more effective representation of complex data. This research offers a significant step towards harnessing the unique characteristics of QIGs for advanced data analysis and modeling tasks.

title: Dynamic Programming for Evolutionary Algorithms with Memory
abstract: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are widely used for solving complex optimization problems. However, EAs often suffer from redundant computations, particularly when exploring large search spaces. This paper proposes a novel approach to enhance the efficiency of EAs by integrating dynamic programming (DP) techniques. The core idea is to introduce a memory component to the EA, allowing it to store and reuse previously computed solutions. This memory is managed using dynamic programming principles, effectively avoiding redundant evaluations. The algorithm maintains a table (or similar data structure) where solutions are indexed by their parameters and the associated fitness value is stored. When a new solution is generated, the algorithm first checks if a similar solution already exists in the memory. If it does, the existing solution is reused, significantly reducing the computational cost. This approach demonstrates a potential improvement in convergence speed and overall efficiency of EAs. The core claim is that incorporating dynamic programming techniques to store and reuse previously computed solutions can enhance the efficiency of evolutionary algorithms.

title: Quantum Entanglement Entropy Transfer
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum information transfer, termed "Quantum Entanglement Entropy Transfer (EET)." The core claim is that by precisely controlling the micro-scale entropy transfer between entangled particles, direct quantum information transmission can be achieved without relying on physical media, circumventing the limitations imposed by classical communication bottlenecks. The proposed mechanism utilizes non-classical thermodynamics and a specifically designed "entropy pump" system. This system leverages microscopic thermal fluctuations within entangled particles to facilitate non-local entropy transfer, thereby driving changes in the entanglement correlation between the particles. Mathematical formalism is presented to describe the entropy transfer process, highlighting the role of entanglement entropy and the thermodynamic parameters governing the system. The novelty of this approach lies in its utilization of entanglement as the primary medium for entropy transfer, coupled with the practical demands of quantum information transmission. The theoretical framework presented offers a potentially transformative pathway for quantum communication, moving beyond conventional approaches and opening avenues for ultra-fast, secure information transfer.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Algorithm Acceleration
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed algorithm acceleration leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core idea is to utilize entangled states to facilitate instantaneous information transfer and collaborative computation between distributed nodes, thereby significantly boosting the performance of existing distributed algorithms. The proposed method addresses the inherent limitations of traditional distributed computing, particularly the bottleneck caused by data transmission delays. We outline a distributed algorithm protocol based on entanglement sharing, where nodes collaboratively process parts of a computational task using the correlated information provided by entangled states. The key challenges lie in the generation and maintenance of stable entanglement across long distances. We explore the theoretical framework and potential benefits of this approach, highlighting its ability to overcome limitations imposed by classical communication. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the potential for achieving exponential speedups in certain distributed algorithms, contingent upon the quality and stability of the entanglement network. Further research will focus on practical implementation strategies and addressing the technological hurdles associated with robust entanglement distribution.

title: Adaptive Lattice Construction (ALC)
abstract: This paper explores the Adaptive Lattice Construction (ALC) system, a novel approach to lattice design leveraging an evolutionary algorithm to automatically generate and refine lattice structures. The core focus is on optimizing for specific properties like connectivity and density, offering a more efficient and adaptable method compared to traditional lattice generation techniques. We present a detailed outline of the ALC system, including the evolutionary algorithm employed, the feedback mechanism that drives refinement, and the mathematical framework underpinning the optimization process. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential applications and benefits of ALC across various domains, particularly in areas requiring complex, structurally-driven mathematical models.

title: Designing GenAI-Supported Adaptive Hypermedia for Classical Chinese Poetry Learning: Expert-Informed Design Considerations
abstract: Learning classical Chinese poetry requires readers to connect lines, imagery, the poet’s biography, place, and historical background. Adaptive hypermedia offers a useful way to organise and guide movement across such linked materials, and generative AI creates new opportunities for adaptive explanation and learner-specific support. It remains unclear, however, how GenAI-supported adaptive hypermedia should be designed for adult poetry learning. We report an expert-informed qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews with 19 participants, including experts in classical Chinese poetry education (n = 11) and experts in GenAI-supported hypermedia design and development (n = 8). Using reflexive thematic analysis, we identify three learning priorities: connected knowledge, cultural-emotional resonance, and sustained interest. We also identify three design challenges: AI answers may be wrong or miss key background, support for different learners remains limited, and learners often receive too little help in building historical and cultural context. Based on these findings, we derive design considerations for GenAI-supported adaptive hypermedia for poetry learning. We then present Poetictok, a prototype that combines place-based exploration, archive cards that learners can reopen later, poem reconstruction tasks, and four role-bounded AI agents. The paper contributes design knowledge for adaptive hypermedia, with particular attention to linked context, adaptive guidance, and visible sources.

title: Substrate-Portable Execution for Production LLM Workflows
abstract: Production LLM agents execute tool-calling loops, retrieval chains, and compositional workflows in multiple modes, yet execution semantics are often coupled to one runtime. We encountered this portability problem in Rufus, a conversational AI assistant with a large tool catalog that serves millions of Amazon customers. Rufus supports real-time serving, asynchronous background tasks, and high-volume batch workloads such as evaluation and content pregeneration. Each mode has distinct service-level objectives and typically uses a separate runtime. Reusing streaming orchestration makes asynchronous and batch workloads blocking and prevents use of batch inference APIs, which offer a 50 percent discount at published prices. We present a binding-adaptive agent execution platform that separates workflow definition from execution substrate. Developers define a workflow once as a typed dataflow graph. The platform compiles the graph to in-process streaming for real-time serving, durable AWS SWF orchestration for asynchronous execution, or distributed Apache Flink stream processing for batch inference. No workflow code changes are required. LLM inference is represented as a suspendable graph node whose behavior depends on the substrate: streaming delivery online, durable retry asynchronously, and batched submission offline. We validated dozens of production agent configurations across five orchestration patterns: single-inference RAG, iterative ReAct, compositional PreAct, conditional routing, and multi-agent deep research. Across all three bindings, we found no detectable difference in output quality. Batch execution reduced per-query inference cost in line with published batch API pricing while operating alongside the streaming path at production scale.

title: A First-Order Learning Algorithm for Online Resource Allocation with Constant Regret
abstract: We study a finite-horizon online resource allocation problem with initial resource capacities proportional to the horizon. In each period, a request type is observed and one action is chosen from a finite menu. Each action earns a reward and consumes a vector of resources. We present a primal first-order learning policy that, in each period, performs one gradient ascent update of the action coordinates associated with one request type, for a fluid relaxation in which resource overuse incurs a quadratic penalty. The policy achieves $O(1)$ expected additive regret relative to the hindsight optimum, with a bound independent of the horizon $T$, under a general arrival model. This model includes independent and identically distributed arrivals with unknown probabilities, independent nonstationary arrivals with known probabilities, independent nonstationary arrivals with unknown probabilities and one historical sample path, and Markov-modulated arrivals with an unknown Markov chain. The policy does not solve any linear program, and the regret bound does not require a nondegeneracy assumption on the fluid linear program.

title: Algorithmic List Decoding at Capacity and Optimal Proximity Gaps for Reed-Solomon Codes
abstract: We give a unified hidden-derivative framework for list decoding and mutual correlated agreement of ordinary Reed--Solomon codes over prime fields, on arbitrary prescribed evaluation sets. For every fixed slack $γ>0$, every sufficiently large block length $n$, every prime $q\ge n$, and every dimension $1\le k\le(1-γ)n$, a deterministic algorithm finds all codewords within relative distance $1-k/n-γ$ in $q^{O_γ(1)}$ time. The final list has size $n^{O_γ(1)}$, independently of $q$. Both statements extend to bounded-input-list recovery, with constants depending additionally on the input-list bound. For every fixed curve degree $\ell$, at most $n^{O_{γ,\ell}(1)}$ parameters on a curve $f_0+zf_1+\cdots+z^\ell f_\ell$ admit a nearby codeword whose exact agreement support is not a maximal jointly explained support of the coefficient words. For lines this gives MCA error $n^{O_γ(1)}/q$, with no proximity loss. The interpolation stage reparameterizes and optimizes the hidden-derivative construction of Brakensiek, Chen, Putterman, Zhang, and Zheng; differential root enumeration uses Kopparty's algorithm. We then prove that a specialization-safe differential equation has a cover by constant-dimensional varieties of polynomial cumulative degree, outside polynomially many parameter values. Intersecting these varieties with equations from the full agreement support yields both the field-size-independent list bound and exact-support MCA.

title: IndicRecipeNutri
abstract: A corpus of 220,187 Indian recipes with multilingual provenance and estimated dish-level micronutrition; a typed knowledge graph of 223,406 nodes and 6,270,560 edges across 17 node types and 21 relation types; a 68-query retrieval benchmark with knowledge-graph-derived gold sets; and a synthetic collaborative interaction log. The food-composition layer uses the IFCT 42-nutrient schema but contains no IFCT and no Indian composition data; its values are USDA SR Legacy and UK CoFID. Two-tier release. Structured, factual and derived fields are published under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 with per-recipe source attribution. Raw recipe prose is not redistributed; a rehydration index of source URLs and SHA-256 text digests is published instead, together with a re-fetch script. Known defects are published, not hidden. An independent allergen and diet audit ships with the data. See the datasheet before use, and do not use the allergen flags for end-user safety decisions.
