title: 基于多模态知识图谱的因果推理
abstract: This paper explores the application of multimodal knowledge graphs for causal inference. Traditional causal inference methods often struggle with complex systems where information is distributed across various modalities, such as text, images, and sensor data. We propose a framework that integrates these diverse data modalities into a unified knowledge graph structure and leverages causal inference algorithms to identify and validate causal relationships. The core claim is that such an approach enhances the accuracy of understanding and predicting complex systems. The mechanism involves the fusion of multimodal information into a knowledge graph, followed by the application of causal reasoning techniques. This work highlights the novelty of combining multimodal knowledge graphs with causal inference, offering a more robust and realistic solution for tackling intricate causal questions. We present a theoretical foundation and outline a potential implementation strategy, emphasizing the key components and their interactions. The resulting system has the potential to improve decision-making in domains requiring a deep understanding of complex interdependencies.

title: Neural Network Topology Adaptive Generation and Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network topology design using reinforcement learning. Traditional methods often rely on pre-defined architectures or biologically-inspired heuristics, limiting the potential for optimal network configurations for specific computational tasks. Our method introduces an automated system where a reinforcement learning agent dynamically generates and optimizes a neural network topology based on a defined task. The agent operates within a simulated neural network environment, receiving rewards based on the efficiency of task execution, such as algorithm execution speed or energy consumption. Through iterative exploration and learning, the agent discovers and refines the network topology, ultimately achieving maximal efficiency. This approach represents a significant departure from mimicking biological neural networks, focusing instead on directly optimizing topology for a given objective. The core claim of this work is that reinforcement learning provides a superior method for designing neural network topologies compared to traditional approaches. The key mechanism involves the construction of a simulated neural network environment and the utilization of a reinforcement learning agent to autonomously generate and optimize the topology.

title: Robustness Evaluation and Detection of Transferable Adversarial Attacks in ML-Based NIDS
abstract: Machine learning-based network intrusion detection systems (ML-based NIDS) are vulnerable to adversarial evasion, where malicious samples are perturbed to evade detection and be misclassified as benign. Despite growing research on adversarial attacks and defenses for ML-based NIDS, comparative evaluations of multiple attack types, detection models, and defense strategies under a common setting remain limited. In this paper, we evaluate eight adversarial evasion attacks, fifteen detection models, and three representative defense strategies using the NF-UQ-NIDS dataset, which includes recent traditional and IoT network traffic with twenty distinct attack categories. The evaluation compares model performance on clean test data and on robustness evaluation sets that include adversarial samples, analyzes attack success consistency across models, and examines the effect of defense strategies on adversarial robustness. To support model comparison, we introduce the Robustness Index (RI), a compact comparative metric that rewards high balanced accuracy and macro-F1 score computed on the robustness evaluation set while penalizing high attack success rate (ASR). We further present AR-NIDS, a two-stage framework that uses an adversarially trained ensemble to distinguish normal, attack, and adversarial samples, followed by an adversarial attack classifier to identify the attack type. Under the evaluated transfer-based setting, the proposed adversarially trained ensemble achieves the strongest overall trade-off between classification performance on the robustness evaluation set and evasion resistance, reducing the average ASR from 0.41 to 0.03 and achieving an RI of 0.98.

evidence.title: Robustness Evaluation and Detection of Transferable Adversarial Attacks in ML-Based NIDS
evidence.abstract: Machine learning-based network intrusion detection systems (ML-based NIDS) are vulnerable to adversarial evasion, where malicious samples are perturbed to evade detection and be misclassified as benign. Despite growing research on adversarial attacks and defenses for ML-based NIDS, comparative evaluations of multiple attack types, detection models, and defense strategies under a common setting remain limited. In this paper, we evaluate eight adversarial evasion attacks, fifteen detection models, and three representative defense strategies using the NF-UQ-NIDS dataset, which includes recent traditional and IoT network traffic with twenty distinct attack categories. The evaluation compares model performance on clean test data and on robustness evaluation sets that include adversarial samples, analyzes attack success consistency across models, and examines the effect of defense strategies on adversarial robustness. To support model comparison, we introduce the Robustness Index (RI), a compact comparative metric that rewards high balanced accuracy and macro-F1 score computed on the robustness evaluation set while penalizing high attack success rate (ASR). We further present AR-NIDS, a two-stage framework that uses an adversarially trained ensemble to distinguish normal, attack, and adversarial samples, followed by an adversarial attack classifier to identify the attack type. Under the evaluated transfer-based setting, the proposed adversarially trained ensemble achieves the strongest overall trade-off between classification performance on the robustness evaluation set and evasion resistance, reducing the average ASR from 0.41 to 0.03 and achieving an RI of 0.98.

title: Pendampingan STEM Terapan melalui Robotika Edukatif untuk Penguatan Literasi Digital Siswa MTs Negeri 9 Pringombo Kabupaten Gunungkidul Yogyakarta
abstract: Literasi digital dan keterampilan teknologi merupakan kompetensi penting yang perlu dikembangkan sejak jenjang pendidikan menengah. Namun, keterbatasan media pembelajaran dan pengalaman praktik teknologi menjadi salah satu tantangan dalam penguatan kompetensi tersebut di sekolah wilayah perdesaan. Kegiatan pengabdian kepada masyarakat ini bertujuan memberikan pengalaman pembelajaran STEM terapan melalui robotika edukatif untuk memperkuat literasi digital dan keterampilan teknologi siswa MTs Negeri 9 Pringombo, Gunungkidul. Kegiatan dilaksanakan pada 17 Juni 2026 dengan melibatkan 25 siswa. Metode pelaksanaan menggunakan pendekatan partisipatif, edukatif, dan learning by doing melalui penyampaian materi, demonstrasi, praktik robotika secara berkelompok, diskusi, dan evaluasi. Siswa dibagi menjadi lima kelompok dan memperoleh pendampingan selama praktik. Evaluasi dilakukan menggunakan kuesioner skala Likert lima tingkat. Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan skor rata-rata keseluruhan sebesar 4,17 atau 83,50% dan termasuk kategori sangat baik. Aspek pemahaman robotika dan coding memperoleh skor 88,94%, ketertarikan dan literasi digital 83,92%, serta manfaat kegiatan 86,47%, sedangkan aspek pelaksanaan pelatihan memperoleh skor 76,58%. Hasil tersebut menunjukkan bahwa kegiatan dapat diterima dengan baik dan memberikan pengalaman positif dalam mengenal robotika dan coding. Kegiatan juga mendapat respons positif dari guru dan sekolah serta menghasilkan rekomendasi untuk pelatihan robotika lanjutan dan penyediaan kit robotika sederhana.

title: Hierarchical Latent Workspace Model: two negative-results preprints
abstract: Two preprints from a twenty-day, ten-experiment preregistered attempt to build a latent-workspace language model: a frozen Qwen3-0.6B decoder wrapped in 73M-132M trainable sidecars implementing a root-preserving expert graph, isolated parallel reasoning lanes, and a private diffusion canvas behind a calibrated publication rule. All three proposed mechanisms failed their preregistered gates. Routing was never causally live in any of ten seed-runs. In the decisive experiment, with the operative premise physically deleted from the decoder's input token ids so the latent channel was the only route from evidence to answer, generation through the channel scored 0.000 on all 99 masked rows on both seeds, while a linear probe recovered roughly 0.30 of the withheld premise. The channel was readable but not usable. Includes a novelty audit of the work's own six architectural claims and an instrument-failure taxonomy with detectors covering roughly thirty documented defects in five classes. The matched plain-LoRA control was never run, so no capability claim is made.

title: Neural Network Topology Automated Optimization and Dynamic Adaptation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network design, leveraging reinforcement learning (RL) to automatically optimize network topology and enable dynamic adaptation to changing tasks. The core idea is to employ an RL agent, guided by a reward function based on network performance, to explore and refine the network's connection topology. We propose a mechanism integrating genetic algorithms or gradient-based optimization with RL, coupled with adaptive learning rates and a dynamic topology adjustment strategy. This approach moves beyond traditional, manually designed topologies or static optimization methods, offering a system capable of self-organizing and adapting to complex, evolving scenarios. The resulting network exhibits enhanced performance and robustness compared to networks with fixed architectures. The key contributions lie in the automated discovery of optimal topologies and the dynamic adjustment of the network structure during training. This research addresses a significant limitation in current neural network design, providing a flexible and efficient framework for tackling diverse and dynamic problems.

title: Automated Theorem Proving with Reinforcement Learning and Symbolic Reasoning
abstract: This paper explores the integration of reinforcement learning (RL) and symbolic reasoning techniques to automate theorem proving. The core idea is to utilize an RL agent to dynamically guide the search process within a traditional theorem prover, adapting its strategy based on the evolving state of the proof. This approach aims to overcome the limitations of purely deterministic or hand-crafted search strategies by learning from experience. The system learns to select proof strategies, optimizing for efficiency. The paper details the architecture, the RL agent's reward function design, and the symbolic reasoning engine utilized. We present a framework for combining these components, aiming to accelerate the discovery of mathematical proofs and potentially expand the scope of automated proof generation. The results, although theoretical at this stage, suggest a promising direction for future research in automated reasoning.

title: Hyper-Adaptive Kernel Learning via Latent Space Exploration
abstract: Kernel methods offer powerful tools for non-linear classification and regression, but their performance is frequently hampered by the sensitivity of kernel parameter selection and their limited adaptability to evolving data distributions. This paper introduces a novel approach, Hyper-Adaptive Kernel Learning (HAKL), that addresses these limitations by leveraging a recurrent neural network to learn a latent space representation of the data. A dynamically adjusted kernel is then constructed based on the latent space projection, enabling continuous adaptation to shifts in the data distribution. Unlike traditional kernel methods that rely on predefined kernel functions, HAKL learns directly from data characteristics, resulting in a more robust and adaptable kernel. The core mechanism is detailed through a series of equations, showcasing the iterative process of latent space exploration and kernel adjustment. The effectiveness of HAKL is demonstrated conceptually, outlining its potential advantages over conventional kernel methods.

title: Title: Adaptive Topological Dynamics
abstract: Adaptive Topological Dynamics (ATD) presents a novel approach to modeling dynamic quantum systems by employing a topological dynamic framework. This framework allows for the simulation of evolving quantum states and systems, providing a unique tool for optimization and machine learning. The core of ATD lies in leveraging the inherent topological properties of quantum systems – specifically, their ability to remain unchanged under continuous transformations – to capture the essential dynamics of quantum behavior. This paper explores the application of ATD to both optimization and machine learning tasks, demonstrating its potential to overcome limitations of conventional methods. The research focuses on the creation of a robust topological structure, the implementation of a dynamic evolution algorithm, and the utilization of the resulting topological features to facilitate efficient and accurate modeling. The fundamental motivation is to provide a more nuanced understanding of quantum behavior through the application of topological principles.

title: Title: Geometric Proof of Algorithm Completeness using Quantum Simulation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to algorithm verification, leveraging the power of quantum simulation to establish completeness. Traditional verification methods often rely on exhaustive testing, which is computationally intractable for complex algorithms. We propose a geometric proof demonstrating the completeness of an algorithm through the simulation of its execution on a quantum computer. This technique offers a fundamentally new pathway to rigorous algorithm validation, potentially enabling the verification of algorithms that are currently beyond the reach of classical methods. The core mechanism involves constructing a geometric structure representing the algorithm's state space, and quantum simulation is used to demonstrate that this structure is fully explored, guaranteeing correctness. The resulting geometric proof provides a rigorous, automated, and computationally feasible method for verifying algorithm completeness.

title: Pseudo-Random Matrix Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on pseudo-random matrices, designed to address the limitations of traditional optimization methods in the face of noisy data and varying gradients. The core mechanism of this algorithm involves dynamically adjusting the matrix parameters based on observed noise and gradient information, enabling a more robust and adaptable optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and experimental validation on several benchmark datasets. The algorithm's adaptability stems from its inherent ability to learn and adjust to complex data distributions, offering a significant advancement in optimization techniques.

title: Title: Bayesian Optimization of Algorithmic Complexity
abstract: This paper explores the application of Bayesian optimization to optimize algorithm complexity, moving beyond static complexity metrics and incorporating a dynamic risk assessment. We propose a self-optimizing framework that leverages Bayesian inference to learn the 'risk' associated with different algorithm configurations, allowing for adaptive adjustments in complexity. The core mechanism involves employing Bayesian methods to model the potential for unexpected behavior, enabling a more robust and adaptable assessment of algorithm suitability. The research addresses a critical gap in complexity analysis by shifting the focus from fixed thresholds to a continuous, risk-aware optimization process. The resulting framework offers a novel approach to algorithm design and performance evaluation, potentially leading to improved efficiency and stability in a wide range of computational tasks.

title: 基于自适应的机器学习的自然语言处理的词语选择
abstract: The task of selecting the most appropriate word from a given set is a fundamental challenge in natural language processing (NLP). Traditional methods often rely on static word lists, failing to effectively handle the dynamic nature of language. This paper introduces a novel approach to word selection based on adaptive machine learning, designed to automatically adjust the selection strategy in response to evolving word context. We propose a method that employs a self-learning algorithm to dynamically refine the chosen word based on subtle shifts in the input text. This allows the system to maintain high accuracy even in complex and nuanced language. The core mechanism revolves around a continuous feedback loop, adjusting the selection weight based on a learned metric that captures the word's contextual relevance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing a significant improvement in word selection accuracy compared to existing methods.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel Neural-Symbolic Fusion Adaptive Learning Algorithm (NSF-AL). The algorithm leverages the synergistic strengths of neural networks and symbolic reasoning to achieve enhanced model learning efficiency. The core mechanism centers around a carefully designed fusion process that intelligently combines the strengths of both neural and symbolic components. This approach overcomes limitations of traditional methods, offering a more adaptable and efficient learning strategy. The algorithm's design emphasizes automated parameter tuning, resulting in superior performance across a range of datasets. This work presents a robust framework for tackling complex tasks requiring both pattern recognition and logical inference.

title: Quantum Information Fusion Theory of Chaos Domains
abstract: Quantum Information Fusion Theory of Chaos Domains explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement to revolutionize the understanding and optimization of chaotic systems. This research focuses on developing a dynamic algorithm predicated on the manipulation of entangled quantum states within a defined chaos domain. The core claim posits that this approach offers a significantly enhanced optimization capability compared to conventional methods, particularly in scenarios requiring rapid adaptation to changing conditions. The proposed mechanism utilizes entanglement to dynamically adjust the characteristics of the chaotic domain, thereby facilitating algorithmic improvements. This paper outlines the theoretical framework, explores the potential challenges, and proposes a preliminary implementation strategy for this novel quantum information fusion approach.

title: Quantum Topological Field Theory: Adaptive Geometry Computation
abstract: Quantum Topological Field Theory (QTTF) offers a novel approach to simulating and optimizing complex geometric fields by introducing an adaptive geometry computation framework. This framework dynamically adjusts geometric features to precisely compute field theory results, eliminating the need for manual geometric model construction. This work presents a new method that leverages the inherent randomness in quantum topological field theory to achieve superior computational efficiency and accuracy. We demonstrate the framework's capabilities through a series of simulations, showcasing its ability to handle intricate geometric configurations with exceptional fidelity. The core mechanism involves establishing a quantum state's geometric topology, dynamically manipulating these topological characteristics, and subsequently calculating field theory outcomes. This represents a significant advancement over traditional geometric computation methods, particularly in scenarios demanding high precision and adaptability.

title: Decentralized Federated Optimization with Byzantine Fault Tolerance using Blockchain
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without directly exchanging the data itself. However, current FL frameworks are susceptible to attacks from malicious participants, known as Byzantine attacks, which can compromise model integrity and potentially inject biases. This paper proposes a novel decentralized federated optimization system leveraging blockchain technology and Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) consensus algorithms to mitigate these vulnerabilities. Our system allows participants to securely contribute model updates and verify their correctness, ensuring a robust and resilient optimization process. The core innovation lies in integrating blockchain's immutability and cryptographic capabilities with BFT to create a system capable of detecting and rejecting malicious updates, thereby safeguarding the global model from manipulation. This approach provides a fundamentally more secure and trustworthy FL environment compared to traditional centralized or even existing decentralized FL methods. We explore the theoretical foundations of this system and outline its key components, focusing on the BFT consensus mechanism and its integration with the FL optimization process. The system's design emphasizes transparency, auditability, and resistance to adversarial attacks, representing a significant advancement in the field of secure and reliable distributed machine learning.

title: Quantum Error Correction Redundancy Codes: Adaptive Encoding
abstract: This paper investigates adaptive encoding strategies for quantum error correction redundancy codes, addressing the limitations of traditional fixed-parameter schemes. The core claim centers on dynamically adjusting the length of the redundancy code and its encoding scheme based on real-time analysis of the error rate within the error correction code. The proposed mechanism utilizes a quantum measurement feedback loop to continuously assess the performance of the error correction code and, subsequently, adjusts encoding parameters. This approach aims to enhance the reliability of quantum information transmission in diverse and complex noise environments. The research introduces a novel framework for self-optimizing quantum error correction, moving beyond static parameters to achieve significantly improved correction capabilities. The theoretical framework and adaptive encoding methodology are presented, illustrating the potential for robust quantum communication systems.

title: MM-SVGEdit: A Multimodal-Driven SVG Editing for UI Design
abstract: In the field of UI design, Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) is widely used as a design medium. However, traditional SVG editing techniques have high entry barriers and require cumbersome manual iteration, while LLM-based editing solutions suffer from low accuracy and poor user controllability. To address these issues, we propose MM-SVGEdit, a multimodal-driven SVG editing approach that integrates traditional SVG editing and LLM-based methods. We introduce a two-stage strategy in which visual grounding is followed by modification. Both stages support two interaction modalities: natural language instructions and direct manipulation (mouse and keyboard). We trained and evaluated MM-SVGEdit on a self-constructed dataset of 14,476 question-answer pairs generated from UIs, covering 11 types of editing operations on both single and multiple UI targets. The results show that MM-SVGEdit improves SVG editing accuracy, efficiency, and user-perceived control while reducing token consumption and response time.

To address these issues, we propose MM-SVGEdit, a multimodal-driven SVG editing approach that integrates traditional SVG editing and LLM-based methods. We introduce a two-stage strategy in which visual grounding is followed by modification. Both stages support two interaction modalities: natural language instructions and direct manipulation (mouse and keyboard). We trained and evaluated MM-SVGEdit on a self-constructed dataset of 14,476 question-answer pairs generated from UIs, covering 11 types of editing operations on both single and multiple UI targets. The results show that MM-SVGEdit improves SVG editing accuracy, efficiency, and user-perceived control while reducing token consumption and response time.

title: Optoelectronic Reservoir Computing with an On-Chip True-Time-Delay Element
abstract: Compact delay elements remain a central challenge in photonic neuromorphic processors. Here, we demonstrate an optoelectronic delayed-feedback reservoir computer that incorporates a foundry-fabricated silicon nitride (Si$_3$N$_4$) true-time-delay circuit within its feedback loop. Eight cascaded Archimedean spirals provide a \SI{1.76}{\metre} on-chip optical path and a calculated passive group delay of \SI{11.63}{\nano\second}. At a feedback gain of $G=0.0223$, the system classifies sinusoidal and square waveforms without error (word error rate, WER\,$=$\,0 across all cross-validation folds), predicts the Mackey--Glass chaotic series with a best-fold normalized mean-square error (NMSE) of $0.0082$, and performs nine-class Japanese Vowels speaker classification with WER\,$=$\,0.0898. We also introduce a subcarrier phase-encoding method that maps the calculated $0.232π$ spiral-to-reference phase contrast onto the measured reservoir states through deliberate aliasing, achieving NMSE\,$=$\,0.0767 and WER\,$=$\,0 without increasing the insertion-loss-limited feedback gain. These results show that on-chip propagation delay in Si$_3$N$_4$ can operate as a functional component of an optoelectronic reservoir computer and motivate lower-loss, more-integrated implementations.

title: Contextual Graph Embeddings via Learned Markov Chains
abstract: Graph embeddings have become a cornerstone of modern graph analysis, enabling machine learning models to effectively process and understand graph-structured data. However, traditional graph embedding techniques often treat nodes as static entities, neglecting the crucial dynamic context that governs their relationships within a graph. This work addresses this limitation by proposing a novel approach – Contextual Graph Embeddings via Learned Markov Chains. We introduce a method for modeling the temporal evolution of nodes by learning Markov chains that predict the likelihood of their neighbors appearing in the immediate future. These learned Markov chain states are then integrated into the graph embedding process, creating representations that capture the dynamic context surrounding each node. Our approach offers a more nuanced and accurate representation of graph data compared to static embedding methods, leading to improved performance in downstream graph-related tasks. The core idea is to represent nodes not just by their inherent features, but also by their evolving relationships within the graph, offering a richer and more informative embedding.

title: 基于多模态数据的知识图谱构建
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to knowledge graph construction that leverages multi-modal data, addressing the limitations of existing methods primarily reliant on structured data. The core claim is that incorporating unstructured data significantly enhances the comprehensiveness of knowledge graphs. The proposed method utilizes Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to extract knowledge from unstructured data sources and integrates this knowledge with structured data through knowledge fusion strategies. The resulting knowledge graph offers a more holistic representation of the underlying domain. We aim to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a detailed theoretical framework, outlining the key components and their interactions. The proposed approach seeks to bridge the gap between disparate data types, creating a richer and more robust knowledge representation. This work contributes to the advancement of knowledge graph construction by providing a framework for effectively utilizing the vast amounts of data available in diverse formats.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Strategies
abstract: This paper investigates the application of evolutionary strategies (ES) to guide the process of symbolic regression. Symbolic regression is a technique used to automatically discover mathematical equations that describe a given dataset. Traditional symbolic regression methods often struggle with complex datasets or require extensive manual parameter tuning. This work proposes a novel approach that integrates ES to optimize the parameters of a symbolic regression engine. The core idea is to use the ES population to explore the parameter space of the regression algorithm, effectively steering the search towards more accurate and interpretable mathematical models. We demonstrate through simulations that this combined approach can yield superior results compared to standard symbolic regression methods, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data and complex relationships. The key formula used in this paper is: f(x) = ∑i=1k ai * xi, where f(x) represents the mathematical function, x is the input variable, and ai are the coefficients to be determined. Furthermore, the evolutionary process is defined by the following equation: xnew = β * xold + ε, where xnew is the new solution, xold is the old solution, β is the guide vector, and ε is the random perturbation. The performance is measured using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), which is calculated as: RMSE = √[ ∑i=1N (yi - ŷi)2 / N ], where yi is the actual value, ŷi is the predicted value, and N is the number of data points.

title: Quantum Random Access Memory for Secure Data Storage
abstract: Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) presents a novel approach to secure data storage by leveraging the inherent randomness of quantum mechanics. This paper explores the core concept of QRAM, focusing on its ability to generate truly random keys for encryption, thereby mitigating the vulnerabilities associated with classical key generation techniques. The core claim is that QRAM's utilization of quantum phenomena provides an unprecedented level of data security. The mechanism relies on harnessing quantum events to produce unpredictable keys, fundamentally addressing a critical weakness in traditional encryption systems. This work outlines the theoretical framework and potential benefits of QRAM, highlighting its capacity to revolutionize data security protocols. The central argument is that moving to a quantum-based key generation system is paramount to securing data in the future.

title: Relational Bayesian Networks with Adaptive Parameter Learning and Structure Refinement
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to building and maintaining Relational Bayesian Networks (RBNs) that leverages adaptive parameter learning and continuous structure refinement. Traditional RBNs often require extensive manual tuning and suffer from inaccuracies due to static parameter assignments and rigid structures. Our method addresses these limitations by dynamically adjusting both the network's parameters and its topology in response to observed data. We employ Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling for parameter estimation and graph cut algorithms for structure refinement. The core claim is that integrating these adaptive mechanisms significantly enhances the accuracy and robustness of RBNs. The proposed framework offers a practical solution for modeling complex, evolving systems where the underlying relationships between variables are not fully known a priori. This work contributes to the advancement of probabilistic graphical models, particularly in scenarios demanding adaptability and precision.

title: Geometric Topology for Adaptive Data Compression
abstract: Geometric topology offers a novel approach to data compression by leveraging the inherent structural properties of data. This paper introduces a new compression algorithm, termed "Adaptive Geometric Compression" (AGC), which dynamically adjusts compression parameters based on the data's topological structure. AGC utilizes a geometric representation of the data to identify and exploit patterns, leading to significant improvements in storage efficiency and transmission speed compared to traditional compression methods. The core mechanism involves constructing a topological representation of the data, which is then used to guide the compression process. This adaptive approach minimizes unnecessary redundancy and optimizes data representation. The implementation demonstrates improved compression ratios and reduced transmission overhead, particularly for data exhibiting complex topological features. The paper further discusses the theoretical underpinnings of AGC, including its geometric structure and the role of the topological representation. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the potential applications of this algorithm in various data storage and transmission scenarios.

title: Title: Geometric Complexity and the Evolution of Cognitive Processes
abstract: This paper explores the intricate relationship between geometric complexity and the evolution of cognitive processes, specifically focusing on memory and attention. We propose a novel methodology leveraging geometric analysis to quantify the complexity of a cognitive system, and subsequently, to predict its temporal evolution. The core claim is that a deeper understanding of the geometry of neural networks—reflected in complexity—is crucial for accurately modeling and forecasting cognitive change. This research contributes to a growing field of cognitive modeling by establishing a quantifiable link between structure and function, potentially offering a pathway towards more robust and predictive models of human cognition. The investigation will examine the impact of various geometric characteristics on memory retrieval and attention span, offering insights into the mechanisms underpinning these processes.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks (SON) Optimization: Leveraging Dynamic Adjustment of Local Activation Functions
abstract: This paper presents a novel optimization strategy for Self-Organizing Neural Networks (SON) based on dynamically adjusted local activation functions. Traditional SON algorithms often rely on static activation functions, which are inadequate for handling complex data distributions. We introduce a mechanism to automatically adjust activation function parameters based on the data distribution, enabling network layer structure adaptation and enhanced generalization performance. The core of this approach involves a dynamically evolving activation function, which optimizes the network's overall structure through iterative adjustment. This allows the network to better capture the underlying data patterns, leading to improved performance on diverse datasets. We detail the proposed method, its theoretical justification, and empirical validation through illustrative examples. This work addresses a critical limitation of existing SON implementations – the dependence on pre-defined activation functions – and offers a promising path toward more robust and adaptable neural network architectures.

This work provides a foundation for future research exploring the transformative potential of combining quantum mechanics with geometric principles.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Causal Discovery from Observational Data
abstract: Causal discovery aims to infer causal relationships from observational data, a critical task in fields ranging from medicine to economics. Traditional approaches often rely on conditional independence tests, which struggle to accurately represent complex, non-linear relationships, particularly in high-dimensional datasets. This paper introduces a novel framework utilizing Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) to address these limitations. The core idea is to evolve a Bayesian network structure over time, explicitly incorporating temporal dependencies present in sequential observational data. We propose a new Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method designed for efficient inference within the evolving DBN structure. The resulting model offers a more robust and accurate representation of causal relationships compared to static conditional independence methods. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through theoretical analysis and outline key considerations for implementation. The primary contribution lies in providing a dynamic, time-aware approach to causal discovery, mitigating the pitfalls of traditional static methods.

title: Nonlinear Time Series Turing Machine Evolution Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel evolutionary algorithm designed to optimize time series Turing machines, focusing on the ability to learn and adapt to evolving data distributions. The core mechanism utilizes a dynamic Turing machine, employing genetic algorithms to dynamically adjust the machine's parameters, enhancing robustness and generalization capabilities. Traditional approaches often rely on fixed rules, which limits their adaptability to complex data environments. This research explores a new paradigm where the algorithm actively learns and responds to data shifts, offering a significant advancement in the design and optimization of these complex systems. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, the core evolutionary process, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating improved performance on a challenging benchmark time series dataset.

abstract: This paper explores the application of fractal geometry to constraint optimization, offering a fundamentally new approach to problem-solving. We propose a novel algorithm that leverages the inherent structure of fractal geometry to represent and manipulate objective functions, enabling solutions beyond traditional geometric approaches. This research focuses on developing a "fractal constraint" algorithm that dynamically evolves a fractal dimension to guide the optimization process, resulting in potential breakthroughs in materials science, computer graphics, and other fields.

title: H2O Dormant Memory: Preregistered Synthetic Evaluations and a Failed Context-Selection Non-Inferiority Test for LLM Agent Swarms
abstract: H2O Dormant Memory is a falsifiable prototype that keeps provenance-bearing memory units outside an active working set until typed cues reactivate a bounded subset. Six preregistered studies evaluated the approach using synthetic or repository-derived data. Early controlled tests reduced active candidates and prompt bytes while preserving quality. The final document-transformation comparison, however, failed its preregistered non-inferiority condition: submitted prompt bytes fell from 41,232 to 5,506, but quality fell from 10/12 to 6/12 because the selector omitted critical numerical evidence and a measurement-status marker. Actual billed tokens, monetary cost, provider-side memory, and energy were not measured. The result is reported as a negative finding and a design requirement for evidence-complete, reversible context selection.

title: Meta-Learning for Algorithm Design and Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of meta-learning techniques to the problem of algorithm design and optimization. Traditionally, meta-learning has focused on learning how to quickly adapt to new *instances* of a given problem. This work proposes a fundamentally different approach: utilizing meta-learning to *learn* the design process itself. We posit that a meta-learner, trained on a diverse set of algorithm design tasks, can acquire a general strategy for algorithm design applicable to unseen problem classes. This approach shifts the focus from simply solving problems to learning *how* to solve them, potentially leading to the discovery of novel and more efficient algorithms. The core claim is that meta-learning can be leveraged to create a system capable of intelligently crafting algorithmic solutions, rather than merely executing pre-defined algorithms. We outline the core mechanism, detailing the training process and the expected outcomes. We discuss the potential impact of this approach on various domains, highlighting its ability to automate and accelerate the algorithm design process.

title: A Review of Machine Learning-Based Time-Series Anomaly Detection in the Water Domain
abstract: Anomaly detection in water-related time-series data often reveals important environmental problems and serves as a starting point for scientific discoveries. Machine learning has become the mainstream method and a research hotspot for anomaly detection in recent years. This review examines 106 research articles from the Web of Science database published over the past 10 years. Unlike other surveys, this review focuses on anomalies arising from the water-related variables themselves rather than from equipment malfunctions. The work assesses the overall trends in the application and development of machine learning models for water-related anomaly detection. It classifies machine learning-based anomaly-detection models from two dimensions: development stage and anomaly-detection paradigm. Our analysis covers the mechanisms, strengths, limitations, and applications of various machine learning-based anomaly-detection models across different paradigms, highlighting current challenges and prospective research directions in water-related anomaly detection.

title: Travel Time Prediction in Supply Chain Management Using Machine Learning
abstract: The purpose of this research is to find data and methods using machine learning and deep learning to correctly predict the estimated travel time for transportation and logistics in a supply chain system. The supply chain ecosystem is very complex and heavily relies on the transportation and logistics of raw materials and finished goods. Accurate travel time estimation is critical because it helps supply chain members to improve logistics consistency and performance. This helps in planning, demand forecasting, lead time management and assembly planning. The logistics on the delivery side of the customer also plays a crucial role in customer satisfaction and voice of customer. With the collection of huge historical data and using novel techniques, the research builds an accurate model to predict travel time of inventory.

title: Distributed Differential Privacy with Adaptive Noise Calibration
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of achieving differential privacy in distributed computing systems, where traditional approaches often suffer from substantial performance overhead due to fixed, potentially excessive, noise calibration. We introduce a novel distributed algorithm that dynamically adjusts noise levels based on the sensitivity of computations. This adaptive calibration mechanism significantly reduces the performance impact while rigorously maintaining differential privacy guarantees. The core innovation lies in a feedback loop that monitors computation progress and adjusts the noise added, optimizing for both privacy and efficiency. We formally define the algorithm and provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating its effectiveness. Our approach represents a substantial improvement over static noise calibration methods and contributes to more practical and efficient distributed differential privacy solutions. The key performance metric is the trade-off between privacy loss (ε) and computational cost (C), which we aim to minimize.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Forced Displacement Broader Than Conflict in Uganda: Robustness Under Distribution Shift and Sparse Labels
abstract: Forced displacement in Uganda extends well beyond conflict-driven flight, encompassing disaster-induced mobility, climate pressures and economic relocation, yet machine learning systems designed to support displaced populations typically assume stable data distributions and abundant labelled examples. We introduce a federated optimisation objective regularised by both differential privacy noise and a distributionally robust penalty, and we prove convergence guarantees under non-identically distributed client data when labels are scarce. The central contribution is a client-weighted aggregation rule that estimates distributional uncertainty without requiring centralised access to raw data, together with a semi-supervised pseudo-labelling mechanism that provably bounds the error introduced by unreliable labels. Theoretical analysis establishes that the proposed method attains sub-linear regret under mild convexity assumptions, while the privacy guarantee degrades gracefully as the number of participating clients grows. The framework is positioned as a methodological foundation for future empirical deployment, with explicit attention to the infrastructural constraints and ethical obligations of humanitarian computing in Uganda.

title: Quantum Noise Dynamic Suppression in Quantum Control Theory
abstract: This paper investigates the dynamic suppression of quantum noise within the framework of quantum control theory. The core challenge in implementing precise quantum operations lies in the significant influence of environmental noise, which introduces uncertainties and degrades control fidelity. We propose a novel approach utilizing real-time feedback control, leveraging quantum sensors to monitor the noise levels within a quantum system. Based on this continuous assessment, control parameters are dynamically adjusted to mitigate the impact of noise. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and mathematical modeling. We aim to enhance the accuracy and stability of quantum control processes, ultimately contributing to the reliable execution of complex quantum operations. The system is described by the following Hamiltonian: $H = H_0 + H_I$, where $H_0$ is the system Hamiltonian and $H_I$ represents the interaction Hamiltonian. The time evolution of the system is governed by the equation: $\frac{d|ψ(t)>}{dt} = \frac{i}{\hbar} [H, |ψ(t)]$. Noise is modeled as a stochastic term, adding to the Hamiltonian: $H = H_0 + H_I + H_N$, where $H_N$ represents the noise Hamiltonian. The control pulse can be described as: $U(t) = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i \, e^{-i\omega_i t}$, where $\alpha_i$ are the amplitudes and $\omega_i$ are the carrier frequencies. The fidelity of the quantum operation is evaluated using the overlap between the initial and final states: $Fidelity = ||^2$. The control parameters are optimized to maximize the fidelity. The quantum state evolution is described by the equation: $|ψ(t+\delta t)> = U(t) |ψ(t)>$, where U(t) is the control pulse. The time-dependent Schrodinger equation is: i/ħ ∂/∂t |ψ(t)> = H|ψ(t)>. The noise introduces uncertainties which can be represented as: $\sigma^2 = - ^2$, where N is the noise operator.

title: Probabilistic Graph Models with Bayesian Inference and Quantum Computing Synergistic Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the synergistic combination of Bayesian inference and quantum computing for optimizing probabilistic graph models. Traditional Bayesian inference, particularly with complex graph structures, faces significant computational challenges. Quantum computing, leveraging its inherent parallelism, offers a promising avenue for accelerating these inference processes. We propose a framework that translates probabilistic graph models into quantum circuits, employing variational quantum algorithms such as Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) or Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) to optimize the model parameters and expedite the inference. This approach aims to enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of Bayesian inference, addressing a critical bottleneck in various applications, including machine learning, statistical inference, and decision-making under uncertainty. The core claim of this research is the effective integration of Bayesian inference and quantum computing to accelerate the inference process. The underlying mechanism involves the transformation of probabilistic graph models into quantum circuits and utilizing quantum algorithms for optimization. This work represents a novel approach to tackling computationally intensive Bayesian inference problems, paving the way for more sophisticated and efficient probabilistic modeling. ---

title: Algorithmic Bias Detection via Differential Information Theory in Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) presents a promising paradigm for training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without direct data sharing. However, this approach is susceptible to algorithmic bias propagation, stemming from inherent differences – differential information – between the local datasets used for training. This paper proposes a novel framework for detecting and mitigating bias in FL systems by leveraging Differential Information Theory (DIT). We develop a method to quantify information loss during the aggregation process, directly attributable to these dataset differences. The resulting information loss metric serves as a diagnostic tool for identifying potential bias sources and informs strategies for mitigating their impact on the global model. Our approach offers a fundamentally new perspective on bias detection within FL, addressing a critical vulnerability in decentralized learning systems. The core claim of this work is that FL systems are vulnerable to algorithmic bias propagation due to differential information between local datasets.

title: How Few Bits Per Amplitude? A Rate–Distortion Floor for Quantum State-Vector Formats, and Where Per-Block Scaling Wins
abstract: Full state-vector simulation of quantum circuits is limited by the memory and bandwidth needed to hold 2^n complex amplitudes. Two published simulators store amplitudes in two bytes rather than sixteen: JUQCS-A (De Raedt et al., 2019), which uses a global linear magnitude grid with an eight-bit phase, and the polar-logarithmic format of Betelú (2020). Betelú closes by asking whether any format uses less storage for a given error. We answer that question. We first establish an information-theoretic floor. The amplitudes of a maximally entangled random state are independent complex Gaussians, so the Shannon rate-distortion bound applies and no format can achieve squared error below 2^-B at B bits per amplitude. Measured against it, JUQCS-A sits 2.17 bits above the floor and Betelú's format 4.21 bits. Block floating point with a shared power-of-two exponent per 32 amplitudes — the MXINT8 layout that current machine-learning hardware executes natively — sits 2.24 bits above it, and 1.20 bits with an exact scale. Block floating point beats JUQCS-A by 1.95x at an exact scale, sits within 17% of it at a power-of-two scale with the ordering set by qubit parity, and beats it on every concentrated state we tested on both metrics. Against Betelú it splits along a boundary we locate and explain. It wins on random states by 3.90x in squared error, a margin that grows as ln N because a global scale is set by an extreme value of the sample. It loses above three or four spikes spread across distinct blocks — the output shape of Shor's algorithm — and it loses the quantum Fourier transform by 2.16x, where Betelú's phase field renders most controlled rotations exact. But the choice of metric decides the winner: across every concentrated state we tested, total variation distance between measurement distributions reverses each squared-error loss, because a block scale flattens amplitudes carrying O(1/N) of the norm that no measurement resolves. All results are at 16-24 qubits on a single core. Every number is produced by a released script. v2 — 2026-09-04 No results or numbers changed from v1. Figure 1: legend moved clear of the curves it was overlapping, and the "Betelú" label in both figure legends corrected — a LaTeX escape had been rendering literally as Betel\'u. Section 4: replaced "per-block scaling recovers most of the remaining gap" with the measured fractions (71% with an exact scale, 47% with a power-of-two scale), which the following paragraph contradicted. Source archive now includes LICENSE and CORRECTIONS.md, so the deposit carries the license it names and the corrections record its README points at.

title: Phase-Aware Multidimensional Reconciliation for Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) relies on efficient information reconciliation to establish identical secret key sequences from correlated modulation data and measurement outcomes. Accurate quadrature measurements are essential for reliable reconciliation, but residual phase mismatch between the signal and local oscillator distorts these measurements in coherent receivers and degrades decoding performance. To improve robustness against residual phase mismatch in homodyne-based CV-QKD, we propose a phase-aware multidimensional reconciliation method that jointly performs syndrome-based low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoding and expectation-maximization-based residual-phase refinement. We derive a discrete-time detection model that explicitly incorporates the receiver’s pulse-dependent quadrature-selection phase and construct phase-dependent virtual observations through multidimensional orthogonal mapping. The LDPC decoder provides posterior information for calculating the posterior spherical-symbol moments used in residual-phase refinement, while the refined phase is fed back to update the virtual observations and decoding likelihoods for the next iteration. Numerical results show that the proposed method achieves a lower residual-phase-estimation RMSE than disclosure-based cross-correlation estimation, BER and FER close to those under perfect phase compensation, and a higher finite-size secret key rate.

title: Rank and classification of $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_8$-linear Hadamard codes
abstract: The $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_8$-additive codes are subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_2^{α_1}\times\mathbb{Z}_4^{α_2}\times\mathbb{Z}_8^{α_3}$. A $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_8$-linear Hadamard code is a Hadamard code which is the Gray map image of such a code. A recursive construction of $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_8$-additive Hadamard codes $\mathcal H^{t_1,t_2,t_3}$, with all $α_i\neq0$, $t_1\geq1$, $t_2\geq0$, and $t_3\geq1$, is known, as are the linearity and kernel of the corresponding codes $H^{t_1,t_2,t_3}$ of length $2^t$. Their rank, however, was not known in closed form. In this paper, we determine $rank(H^{t_1,t_2,t_3})$ for every admissible triple and obtain an explicit closed formula. The proof computes the dimension of the space spanned by the binary coordinate functions of the code, viewed as Boolean functions of the binary digits of the message. We then use the rank formula, together with the known kernel dimension, to classify the family as far as these two invariants allow. The only pairs of distinct types of the same length sharing both invariants are $\bigl(H^{1,2,t-6},H^{2,0,t-5}\bigr)$ for $t\geq7$ and $\bigl(H^{2,2,t-9},H^{3,0,t-8}\bigr)$ for $t\geq10$. Consequently, the number of distinct pairs $(r,k)$ among the codes of length $2^t$ is $\lfloor(t^2+6)/12\rfloor$ for $3\leq t\leq6$, $\lfloor(t^2+6)/12\rfloor-1$ for $7\leq t\leq9$, and $\lfloor(t^2+6)/12\rfloor-2$ for $t\geq10$. Thus, rank and kernel dimension classify the family completely if and only if $3\leq t\leq6$. We also determine all coincidences with the $\mathbb{Z}_4$-, $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4$-, and $\mathbb{Z}_8$-linear Hadamard codes of the same length: there is exactly one infinite family with the first two, namely $H^{2,1,t-7}$ and $H^{5,t-9}$ for $t\geq10$, and exactly five families with the $\mathbb{Z}_8$-linear codes.

title: Sparse Incident-Cluster Learning for 12-hour Port Flood Pre-warning in Digital-Twin Analytics
abstract: Port flood digital twins require analytics that warn operators before disruption, but official warning incidents are often few and adjacent observations are temporally dependent. Row-level classification can therefore overstate performance by placing windows from the same event in both model-development and evaluation data. We formulate 12-hour port flood pre-warning as an incident-cluster learning problem and evaluate a digital-twin analytics module using eight-point water-level histories, prediction-time contextual covariates, and interpretable short-window dynamics. The protocol combines fold-specific sparse feature selection, warning-cluster grouping, negative-label controls, 100-repeat random top-k controls, and alert-episode evaluation. Liverpool is the primary four-cluster case study, with harmonised Humber/Hull-proxy and Wessex South data used for protocol-transfer checks. Across the Liverpool folds, the top-10 ElasticNet model achieves mean F2 = 0.696, compared with 0.633 without top-k truncation and 0.681 for full-feature weighted XGBoost. It is the strongest ElasticNet variant, remains competitive with the nonlinear reference using only ten predictors, and exceeds the repeat-level 95th percentile of broad and same-family random subsets. Contextual covariates provide a strong prediction-time anchor, complemented by physically interpretable local dynamics. Historical replay converts risk scores into alert episodes and measures alert duration and false-episode burden. The result is an offline-evaluated analytics and validation module designed for integration into a port digital twin.

title: Broken on Arrival: Silently Defective LLM Artifacts in Public Model Registries and How to Catch Them
abstract: Developers increasingly run large language models locally by pulling quantized GGUF artifacts from public registries, yet nothing in the distribution pipeline functionally tests these conversions before they reach users. We executed 327 quantized code-capable model artifacts: 305 from the official Ollama library, spanning 15 model lines at every eligible quantization level at or under 8 GB, and 22 from the most-downloaded community repositories on HuggingFace. Each ran a 15-task smoke suite calibrated so that healthy artifacts pass while a known-broken one fails; suspects then faced full 164-task evaluation, a second inference backend, an independent distributor's conversion of the same model and quantization as referee, and, for community files, re-testing under the artifact's own template. The official library carries five silently defective artifacts, a batch of four Qwen2.5-Coder-3B conversions and one phi3.5-mini conversion, that solve zero of 164 tasks and zero of the smoke suite on both backends while independent conversions of the same models work: 1.6% of official artifacts, 2 of 29 model-and-size conversion groups. The adjudication chain cleared small-model artifacts that a naive threshold would condemn as broken when they are merely collapsed by extreme quantization, and it exposed two older community conversions that degrade badly on CUDA yet pass on Metal: not defective files but backend-dependent failures, a third phenomenon no registry currently tests for. Two confirmed defects produce output whose surface statistics sit inside the healthy range, invisible to any low-noise heuristic short of execution. We release the audit dataset, the quantcheck acceptance-testing tool, and disclosure reports for every confirmed defect (https://github.com/aditi-p31/quantcheck), and argue that model registries need the acceptance gate that package registries already run.

title: Resonant Neural Networks for Continuous Control with Periodic Perturbations
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to continuous control problems utilizing resonant neural networks. The core idea revolves around designing neural network architectures that inherently respond to periodic perturbations, enabling them to resonate at specific frequencies and exert precise control over continuous systems. Traditional control methods often struggle with systems exhibiting periodic disturbances, requiring complex tuning and potentially leading to instability. Resonant neural networks offer a fundamentally different strategy, leveraging the network's dynamic properties to adapt and counteract these perturbations. This work details the architecture design, the underlying principles of resonance, and demonstrates the potential of this technique for achieving robust and efficient continuous control. We introduce a framework where the network's internal dynamics are tuned to match the periodic perturbation, allowing for a direct and effective control response. The effectiveness of this approach is illustrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, highlighting the advantages over conventional control strategies. Further research and development are anticipated to explore the practical implementation and scaling of this resonant neural network concept.

title: Formalizing and Verifying the Security of Secure Multi-Party Computation Protocols
abstract: Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) enables computations to be performed on sensitive data without revealing the underlying data itself. However, the security proofs for SMPC protocols frequently involve intricate designs and heavily depend on strong cryptographic assumptions, posing significant challenges for implementation and understanding. This paper introduces a novel approach to formalizing and verifying the security of SMPC protocols by leveraging process calculus. We develop a formalized framework to represent SMPC protocols as process systems, facilitating rigorous analysis and verification of their security properties. This methodology reduces the reliance on complex cryptographic assumptions, offering a more transparent and robust security assurance. The core of this work lies in the construction of a process calculus model that accurately captures the interaction between parties involved in an SMPC protocol, allowing for the systematic identification and elimination of potential vulnerabilities. We demonstrate the applicability of this framework through a case study, showcasing its ability to uncover subtle security flaws that might otherwise be missed during traditional security analyses. The presented approach contributes significantly to the advancement of SMPC security by providing a practical and verifiable method for ensuring protocol correctness and robustness.

title: Graph Generative Adversarial Networks for Synthetic Data Generation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to synthetic data generation leveraging Graph Generative Adversarial Networks (G-GANs). The core idea is to utilize a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture specifically designed for generating graph structures. The generator network learns to produce synthetic graphs that mimic a target distribution, while the discriminator network attempts to distinguish between real and synthetic graphs. This method addresses the critical need for training machine learning models, especially in data-scarce domains, by providing a means to create realistic synthetic graph datasets. We explore the architectural design of the G-GAN, focusing on the generator and discriminator components, and discuss the training process. The results demonstrate the potential of G-GANs in generating high-quality synthetic graph data, offering a viable alternative to traditional data augmentation techniques. The key contribution lies in the application of GANs to graph data generation, leading to a more effective and flexible approach compared to existing methods.

title: Algorithmic Transparency and Explainable AI via Symbolic Regression
abstract: The increasing complexity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, particularly deep neural networks, poses significant challenges in understanding and trusting their decisions. Traditional explainable AI (XAI) methods often provide post-hoc justifications that can be misleading or lack genuine insight into the model's reasoning process. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging symbolic regression to achieve algorithmic transparency and generate truly explainable AI. The core idea is to train a symbolic regression system on the internal representations of a pre-trained neural network. This allows the symbolic regression system to automatically derive human-readable mathematical equations that approximate the neural network's behavior, effectively revealing the model's underlying logic. We demonstrate that this approach offers a direct, interpretable representation of the model's reasoning, moving beyond the limitations of black-box explanations. The generated equations provide a clear and concise understanding of the decision-making process, enhancing trust and facilitating further analysis and refinement of the AI model.

title: Probabilistic Symbolic Regression with Causal Discovery
abstract: Symbolic regression is a powerful technique for discovering mathematical expressions from data. However, it is prone to identifying spurious correlations, leading to models that may not generalize well or be easily interpreted. This paper proposes a novel approach to probabilistic symbolic regression that integrates causal discovery techniques. The core idea is to leverage causal discovery algorithms, such as the PC algorithm, to prune the search space of symbolic regression, focusing on variables with demonstrable causal influences. This hybrid approach aims to mitigate the issue of spurious correlations and produce more robust and interpretable models. The method introduces a probabilistic framework, allowing for uncertainty quantification throughout the regression process. We outline the key components of this approach and discuss its potential benefits in various applications. The core claim is that integrating causal discovery techniques can significantly improve symbolic regression by identifying true causal relationships, leading to more reliable and understandable models. This paper provides a foundational framework for future research in this area. ---

title: Core Claim: This paper explores the application of a dynamically extended topological structure to SOM, enabling the identification and modeling of high-dimensional data with automated optimization and feature extraction.
abstract: The Self-Organizing Map (SOM) is a powerful unsupervised learning technique, widely employed for dimensionality reduction and data clustering. However, traditional SOM implementations often rely on static representations, limiting their ability to effectively model complex, high-dimensional datasets. This paper introduces a novel approach to SOM – a dynamically extended topological structure – that dynamically adjusts the topology of the map during training, facilitating the identification of meaningful patterns and the automated optimization of data representations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through the application of SOM to a dataset of high-dimensional physiological signals, demonstrating improved clustering accuracy and automated feature extraction compared to existing methods. The core mechanism involves the iterative adjustment of the map's topology based on the input data, resulting in a more robust and adaptable representation.

title: Adaptive Probabilistic Model
abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Probabilistic Model, an innovative approach to probabilistic modeling designed to automatically adjust model parameters and assumptions based on observed data. The core mechanism centers around a dynamic probability adjustment process, ensuring that the model remains optimally calibrated and capable of capturing complex system dynamics. The model's ability to adapt to changing conditions represents a significant advancement over static probability models, offering improved accuracy, robustness, and generalization capabilities. This work demonstrates the efficacy of this framework through a comprehensive analysis and illustrative examples, highlighting its potential to address challenges in diverse scientific and engineering applications.

title: Quantum Information Fields: Adaptive Mapping
abstract: Quantum information fields are a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics, and their study has garnered significant attention due to their potential for revolutionary advancements in computation and communication. This paper explores the concept of adaptive mapping, a novel approach to quantum information field design that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust the field's characteristics, thereby enhancing both quantum computing efficiency and quantum communication security. The core aim is to exploit the inherent responsiveness of quantum systems to external influences, offering a pathway towards more robust and versatile quantum technologies. We detail the design of a specific adaptive mapping framework, outlining its theoretical underpinnings and potential practical applications. This work addresses a critical gap in current research by focusing on the integration of entanglement into a dynamic field adjustment mechanism. The resulting system promises to overcome limitations in existing approaches, potentially unlocking new frontiers in quantum information processing and security.

title: Non-Linear Constraint Optimization via Fractal Mapping
abstract: This paper presents a novel method for non-linear constraint optimization, leveraging fractal mapping to effectively navigate complex solution spaces. Traditional optimization techniques often struggle with the inherent difficulty of these landscapes, limiting their applicability to specific problem types. We introduce a fractal mapping approach that transforms the optimization problem into a fractal domain, enabling efficient exploration and improved performance compared to conventional methods. This work demonstrates the potential of fractal mapping to address challenges in various optimization domains, particularly those involving intricate constraints and complex geometries. The core mechanism focuses on utilizing fractal geometry to represent the landscape, facilitating the identification of promising regions for solution exploration.

title: A Pre-Training Diagnostic for Amplitude-Encoding Failure in Quantum Classifiers, with Validated Symmetry-Breaking Remedies
abstract: Simulator-only study of when amplitude-encoded variational quantum classifiers fail, with validated fixes. Real amplitude encoding obeys rho(x) = rho(-x). When preprocessing (typically z-scoring) drives class means antipodal, encoded classes collapse and a loss barrier appears. This work provides a one-pass pre-training risk score (class-mean cosine, with class-mean trace distance T and a linear probe) plus three A/B-tested symmetry-breaking remedies. Headline: class-mean cosine predicts classical-minus-QNN balanced-accuracy gap across 15 public binary datasets at Spearman rho = -0.72 (dataset-permutation p = 0.0034), with 10 datasets held out from calibration. Fixed binary cutoffs do not transfer as universal constants; the transferable instrument is the continuous score. Remedies recover selectively on flagged datasets (breast cancer 0.784 → 0.961, d_z up to 6.5). Synthetic sweep isolates mechanism (Spearman 1.0, classical at ceiling). All exact statevector, verified to ~1e-7. title: 超分辨率几何分析 - 几何变换的量子计算应用
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing to revolutionize geometric analysis, specifically focusing on the application of quantum algorithms to enhance super-resolution techniques. We address the limitations of traditional methods and propose a novel quantum-based algorithm designed to accelerate image reconstruction and improve the efficiency of geometric transformations. The core claim is that leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition will lead to significant computational advantages, particularly in scenarios requiring rapid and precise geometric manipulation. This research investigates the feasibility of this approach and outlines the potential benefits, including enhanced speed and the exploration of novel computational pathways. The study will present a preliminary analysis of the algorithmic design and potential optimization strategies.

title: Dynamic Topology for Quantum Geometry Computation Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum geometry computation framework based on dynamic topology. We propose a method for constructing and manipulating quantum geometric structures using quantum entanglement, enabling highly accurate and efficient geometric calculations. The framework leverages the inherent properties of dynamic topology to generate complex geometric patterns with minimal computational cost. The core mechanism involves establishing and maintaining entanglement between multiple quantum systems, which provides a pathway for complex geometric transformations. This approach overcomes the limitations of traditional geometric computation, offering the potential for significant advancements in geometric modeling and analysis. This work aims to provide a robust and scalable computational tool for exploring and manipulating quantum geometric data.

Traditional quantum state simulation methods often rely on static models, limiting their ability to represent complex quantum phenomena and hindering optimization for quantum computation. We propose a new approach that dynamically adjusts the geometric representation of the quantum system, enabling a more precise and efficient simulation. The core mechanism involves the application of dynamic geometric transformations to represent the system's evolution, coupled with a quantum optimization algorithm to enhance simulation accuracy and speed. We present preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's improved performance in simulating specific quantum states and showcasing its potential for optimizing quantum algorithm design.

title: Hypergraph Neural Networks for Representing Multi-Relational Data
abstract: This paper introduces Hypergraph Neural Networks (HGNNs) as a novel approach to representing and learning from data exhibiting complex multi-relational dependencies. Traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) operate under the restrictive assumption of a single-relational graph structure, inherently limiting their ability to capture intricate relationships within data. HGNNs address this limitation by leveraging hypergraphs, which allow edges to connect multiple nodes concurrently. This expansion enables the direct modeling of multi-relational data, leading to richer feature representations and improved learning outcomes. We propose a framework for constructing and utilizing HGNNs, detailing the key architectural components and learning strategies. The core claim is that HGNNs provide a more expressive model for data with complex relationships than traditional GNNs. We demonstrate the potential of HGNNs through a theoretical analysis, focusing on the inherent advantages of the hypergraph structure and the impact on information propagation. The model is described using the following notation: Let *H* be a hypergraph with *V* = {*v*1, *v*2, ..., *v*N} (nodes) and *E* = {(*v*i, *v*j, ..., *v*k)} (hyperedges), where *N* is the number of nodes and *K* is the maximum size of a hyperedge. The representation of a hyperedge *e* = (*v*i, *v*j, ..., *v*k) is denoted as *e* = (*r*i, *r*j, ..., *r*k), where *r*i, *r*j, ..., *r*k are the feature vectors associated with the nodes in that hyperedge. The message passing process can be represented as: *m*i = Σj∈N(i) αij *r*j, where *m*i is the message from node *v*i, *N(i)* is the set of nodes connected to *v*i, and αij is the attention weight between nodes *v*i and *v*j. The updated representation for node *v*i is then calculated as: *r*i(l+1) = (1-αi) *r*i(l) + αi *m*i, where αi is the hyperactivation factor. This approach aims to provide a foundational understanding of HGNNs and their potential applications.

title: Quantum-Inspired Kernel Design for Support Vector Machines
abstract: Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are powerful machine learning models widely used for classification and regression tasks. However, their performance can be significantly impacted by the choice of the kernel function, which defines how data points are mapped into a higher-dimensional space. Traditional kernels often struggle to capture complex, non-linear relationships effectively, leading to suboptimal results. This paper proposes a novel approach to kernel design inspired by quantum mechanical principles. Specifically, we leverage concepts of quantum entanglement and superposition to generate kernels that can potentially capture richer and more nuanced data patterns. Our core claim is that employing these quantum-inspired designs can improve SVM performance and scalability. We present a theoretical framework outlining how quantum mechanical effects can be translated into kernel functions. The proposed method is based on constructing kernel functions that implicitly encode correlations between data points, mimicking the inherent interconnectedness observed in quantum systems. We explore specific kernel formulations based on these principles and discuss their potential advantages and challenges. The ultimate goal is to demonstrate that quantum inspiration can unlock new avenues for kernel design, leading to more effective SVM models.

title: 基于异质性自适应的量子算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm, termed "Heterogeneous Self-Adaptive Quantum Algorithm" (HSQA), designed to enhance quantum algorithm performance through dynamic parameter and strategy adjustment based on the inherent properties of different quantum systems and quantum operations. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on static parameter settings, hindering adaptability and optimization. HSQA achieves this adaptation by intelligently selecting and modifying quantum operations to optimally leverage the strengths of various quantum hardware configurations. The core mechanism involves a self-tuning process that continuously analyzes the system's state and adjusts quantum operations to maximize fidelity and efficiency. This approach promises significant improvements over existing algorithms, particularly in scenarios involving complex quantum systems and diverse operational parameters. This work presents a framework for automated parameter optimization and explores its impact on various quantum computing tasks.
