title: A Ghanaian pre-SHS feasibility study of AI chatbots as more knowledgeable others for supporting science learning in a resource-constrained context
abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence offers innovative potential for personalised learning, yet its integration remains hindered by instructional voids and restrictive mobile-device policies globally. This study addresses these challenges by investigating AI-powered chatbots as a scalable scaffolding tool for science learning in resource-constrained settings where a scarcity of personalised instructional resources presents a significant barrier to science outcomes. Employing a pre-experimental single-group pre-test/post-test design, the research assessed changes in cognitive outcomes and holistic competencies among 31 pre-Senior High School students in Ghana using researcher-developed, validated instruments. The intervention integrated the chatbot as a self-directed learning and inquiry support system over four weeks. Qualitative data were analysed thematically and subsequently quantified. Quantitative data were analysed using paired t-tests and the robust Wilcoxon signed-rank test, supplemented by Spearman’s rank-order correlation and Least Absolute Deviations (LAD) regression. Findings revealed statistically significant improvements across the measured domains, with large effect sizes observed for cognitive outcomes (Cohen’s d > 2.0) and moderate-to-large effect sizes for holistic outcomes (Wilcoxon r = 0.41–0.68). The findings suggest that the chatbot functioned as a More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) within the structured learning intervention and may have supported cognitive and self-directed learning processes, consistent with Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT) interpretations. Critically, the study found a strong positive correlation (ρ > 0.8) between students’ learning outcomes and their self-reported Perception of Utility. This research provides preliminary evidence on the feasibility and potential value of AI-supported learning for expanding personalised learning opportunities in resource-constrained educational contexts.

title: How to Learn from What a Human Would Avoid? Intervention-Aware World Models with Real-World RL for Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: Multi-fingered dexterous manipulation remains a frontier for real-world reinforcement learning (RL) due to the high-dimensional action space and the prohibitive cost of hardware failures. While human-in-the-loop (HIL) RL allows operators to intervene before failures occur, current pipelines often treat these interventions as reactive corrections, discarding the rich safety signal inherent in the operator's decision to take control. In this paper, we ask: How can we learn from what a human would avoid? We present WHIRL, a safety-aware RL framework that transforms binary human interventions into forward-predictive signals for proactive risk avoidance. Our approach centers on an intervention-aware latent world model with four prediction heads: dynamics, reward, termination, and a novel per-state intervention-probability head that learns to predict the likelihood of a human takeover at future states. This head provides an actor-side risk-shaping term that discourages the policy from entering "intervention-prone" regions, modeling the operator's internal safety threshold. We evaluate our framework on a 16-DoF LEAP Hand across tasks spanning convex and irregular object grasping, prismatic manipulation, and long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Our results show that predictive risk-shaping enables the system to achieve a 96.7 percent success rate on complex grasping tasks while reducing the operator intervention burden by up to 84 percent in step-weighted terms. By closing the loop between human intuition and predictive world modeling, this work provides a practical safety-aware recipe for training complex dexterous agents in the real world while reducing operator fatigue and hardware-risk exposure.

By closing the loop between human intuition and predictive world modeling, this work provides a practical safety-aware recipe for training complex dexterous agents in the real world while reducing operator fatigue and hardware-risk exposure.

title: Hierarchical Prompt Injector for Domain Generalization Segmentation
abstract: Domain Generalized Semantic Segmentation (DGSS) is a challenging task, as vision models often rely on low-level appearance cues that change across domains. In contrast, structural attributes exhibit cross-domain stability, motivating the use of structural priors for DGSS. Existing methods use prompt learning to transfer such priors into DGSS models, but typically encode each class as a single holistic prompt. Moreover, these methods apply prompts uniformly to all pixels, offering no mechanism to adapt when only a subset of object regions is visible due to viewpoint changes, occlusion, and environmental variation. We address this with \textbf{Spatial Hierarchical Prompts (SHP)} that enrich each class with region-level geometric anchors capturing structural appearance from distinct viewing angles, ensuring complementary coverage under arbitrary viewpoints. Additionally, we propose the \textbf{Hierarchical Prompt Injector (HPI)}, which enables spatially adaptive prompt injection in foundation models. HPI spatially grounds prompts by modeling their semantic relevance and spatial influence with visual features. Considering the difficulty of learning spatially and semantically aware prompt injection, we further introduce auxiliary supervision to align hierarchical prompts with their corresponding object regions. We achieve 70.62\% and 72.74\% mIoU on synthetic-to-real and real-to-real benchmarks, respectively. Code and checkpoints are released at https://github.com/MosukFate/HPI

title: MFCMd: Multivariate Fuzzy C-Medoids Clustering
abstract: MFCMd combines medoid-based prototypes with multivariate membership degrees, improving robustness to noise and outliers while accounting for the relevance of each variable within each cluster. title: Verus Phase 37
abstract: Phase 37 of the Verus project — the Dynamic Integrity Engine — is the runtime enforcement layer beneath the constitutional principles laid out in the Cosmic Compact. Where a constitutional framework states what an AI system must respect, Phase 37 is the mechanism that continuously checks a running system's actual evidentiary state against those commitments and produces a cryptographically verifiable, tamper-evident record of that checking. The engine converts observed evidence — about a system's authority, risk posture, operating conditions, and stakeholder alignment — into an integrity state, resolved through a strict precedence order (failure > authority > conflict > material > unresolved > delta > current), and deterministically routes that state to one of seven runtime actions ranging from CONTINUE to FAIL_SAFE. This paper documents the engine's architecture across its constituent modules (Phases 37.15–37.20): its evidence-integrity guarantees (deterministic canonicalization, hash-linked lineage, mutation-after-seal detection), its cryptographic attestation layer (Ed25519-signed, chained certificates with key rotation), its durability under restart and partial failure, and two hardening case studies — a SQL-identifier injection defect and a canonicalization coverage gap — each documented as found, fixed, and regression-tested rather than omitted. The paper closes with an explicit statement of what "verified" means in this context (internal, first-party, adversarial self-testing) and what remains for independent third-party audit. This is the third paper in the Verus series, following Phase 35 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20586883) and Phase 36 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21246720).

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization of Genetic Algorithms for Complex Search Spaces
abstract: This paper explores the integration of quantum-inspired concepts into Genetic Algorithms (GAs) to improve their performance in complex search spaces. Traditional GAs often struggle with the computational cost of evaluating numerous candidate solutions, particularly in high-dimensional spaces. We propose a novel approach where candidate solutions are represented in a superposition of states, mimicking the quantum mechanical principle of superposition. Furthermore, we introduce tunneling mechanisms to enable rapid traversal of the search space, inspired by the quantum tunneling effect. The core idea is to leverage the ability of quantum systems to exist in multiple states simultaneously, allowing the GA to explore a wider range of potential solutions concurrently. The implementation details and the theoretical underpinnings of this hybrid approach are presented, demonstrating the potential for significant acceleration in GA convergence and solution quality. The efficacy of this quantum-inspired GA is demonstrated through an analysis of its performance compared to standard GAs on several benchmark problems, illustrating its ability to overcome limitations inherent in traditional evolutionary algorithms. The key contribution lies in the combined application of superposition and tunneling, offering a new paradigm for optimizing GAs.

title: Explainable AI for Deep Reinforcement Learning through Counterfactual Analysis
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents have achieved remarkable success in various domains, from game playing to robotics. However, their internal workings are often opaque, presenting a significant challenge for trust, verification, and debugging. This work proposes a novel approach to explain the decision-making processes of DRL agents by leveraging counterfactual analysis. We introduce a methodology that generates counterfactual scenarios – minimal changes to the input state – and observes the resulting agent actions. This allows us to identify which factors were most influential in the agent's decision, effectively revealing the underlying policy and decision boundaries. The core claim is that by examining these counterfactuals, we can transform these black-box agents into more transparent and understandable systems. This approach offers a practical and interpretable method for understanding DRL agent behavior, opening avenues for improved design, safety, and robustness.

title: Algorithmic Transparency and Explainability via Formal Model Checking of Neural Networks
abstract: The increasing deployment of neural networks in critical applications, such as autonomous driving and medical diagnosis, raises significant concerns regarding transparency and explainability. The "black box" nature of these networks makes it difficult to understand their decision-making processes, leading to a lack of trust and hindering widespread adoption. This work proposes a novel approach to enhance algorithmic transparency and explainability by leveraging formal model checking techniques. We develop a formal model of a neural network and utilize model checking to rigorously verify its properties, including robustness against adversarial attacks and adherence to predefined constraints. The verification process generates detailed explanations based on the model checking results, providing insights into the network's behavior. This approach offers a rigorous and quantifiable method for ensuring the reliability and trustworthiness of neural networks, addressing a critical gap in current practices. The core claim is that a lack of transparency in neural networks hinders trust and adoption, and formal model checking provides a rigorous method for verifying network behavior.

title: 基于本体论的动态知识图谱推理
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to knowledge reasoning utilizing a dynamic knowledge graph (DKG) grounded in an ontology. The core claim is that leveraging the semantic relationships within an ontology and the evolutionary mechanisms of a DKG can significantly enhance the flexibility and accuracy of inference capabilities. The proposed system employs a rule engine based on the ontology to drive dynamic reasoning and a suite of graph algorithms operating on the DKG to facilitate knowledge discovery. This integration offers a more intelligent method for both knowledge inference and knowledge management compared to traditional approaches. The system is designed to adapt to evolving knowledge landscapes, addressing limitations of static knowledge graphs. This paper details the architecture, algorithms, and key components, outlining a framework for building and operating such a system. The presented methodology provides a foundation for developing robust and adaptable knowledge reasoning systems, particularly in domains characterized by rapid change and complex relationships. ---

title: Title: Dynamic Adaptive Topology Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology-based algorithm designed for the modeling of complex and evolving systems. Traditional approaches to system representation often rely on manually adjusted parameters, limiting their adaptability to dynamic environments. Our algorithm leverages a dynamically adjustable topology network, allowing the system to proactively adapt to changing input data and evolutionary pathways. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations, showcasing its ability to achieve higher levels of self-adaptation and scalability compared to traditional methods. This work represents a significant advancement in system representation and modeling, offering a promising path towards more robust and versatile system design.

title: Geometric Information in Quantum Algorithms
abstract: Geometric information, a fundamental concept in geometry, offers a novel perspective for enhancing quantum algorithms. This paper explores the potential of integrating geometric information into quantum algorithms, focusing on the design of a quantum algorithm specifically optimized for leveraging geometric structures. We present a new approach that utilizes geometric information to improve both the efficiency and reliability of quantum computations. The core mechanism centers on embedding geometric structures within the algorithm's structure, facilitating information transfer and computation in a more structured and predictable manner. This approach addresses a longstanding challenge in quantum algorithm design, promising significant improvements in performance and robustness.

We address the challenges of simulating complex biological molecular structures, highlighting the unique capabilities of quantum algorithms that promise to revolutionize drug discovery, protein engineering, and fundamental biological research. This work focuses on utilizing quantum entanglement to accelerate molecular modeling and introduces a novel approach based on quantum algorithms for protein structure prediction, demonstrating significant advancements in computational efficiency and accuracy. The paper presents a detailed overview of the core claim, mechanism, and potential applications of this emerging field.

title: High-Level Quantum Information Cryptography – Based on Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement as a foundation for a novel cryptographic system, termed "Logical Defense Cryptography." The core principle revolves around encoding information within entangled quantum states, aiming to create a defense against classical cryptanalysis. We investigate the feasibility of exploiting quantum entanglement to generate irreversible data modifications, thereby hindering traditional decryption methods. The research focuses on establishing a robust and demonstrably secure system, leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics. This paper will present a preliminary assessment of the system's potential, highlighting key challenges and future research directions.

title: Self-Adaptive Quantum Entanglement Computing Model
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for revolutionizing computation. However, harnessing this potential requires sophisticated computational techniques, particularly in the realm of quantum information processing. This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive quantum entanglement computing model that dynamically adjusts the entangled state to optimize computational efficiency and precision. We propose a mechanism for continuous state adjustment, leveraging a feedback loop to minimize errors and maximize the utility of entangled qubits. The model's design is predicated on the principle of optimizing entanglement characteristics for specific computational tasks. The core claim of this work is that this self-adaptive approach significantly improves the performance of quantum algorithms, particularly in scenarios requiring high fidelity and reduced error rates. The paper details the model's architecture, the implemented dynamic adjustment mechanism, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its efficacy.

title: Generative Relational Databases with Variational Autoencoders
abstract: The creation of realistic and diverse relational databases remains a significant challenge in data science and artificial intelligence. Traditional methods of generating synthetic data often struggle to capture the complex relationships and constraints inherent in relational data, leading to datasets that lack realism and diversity. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to address this problem. The core idea is to train a VAE to learn the latent distribution of real-world relational data, effectively capturing the underlying structure and dependencies. This learned latent space can then be sampled to generate new, synthetic relational databases that closely resemble the original data. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a detailed exploration of the VAE architecture, training process, and evaluation metrics. The generated databases are assessed for realism and diversity, highlighting the potential of VAEs for creating high-quality synthetic relational data. Key challenges and future directions are discussed, including scaling the approach to larger and more complex datasets and incorporating domain-specific knowledge.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Self-Organization Control Based on Quantum Topology Networks
abstract: Quantum self-organization (QSO) networks offer a promising platform for enhancing the stability and complexity of quantum devices. This paper introduces an adaptive quantum self-organization control framework utilizing dynamic network restructuring, aiming to achieve robust and sophisticated quantum performance. We propose a novel method for dynamically adjusting the network topology, leveraging quantum self-organization principles to mitigate inherent vulnerabilities and enhance device control. This approach addresses limitations of static topology-based networks by providing a flexible and responsive control mechanism. The fundamental concept revolves around constructing a network that evolves based on internal quantum states, allowing for targeted adjustments to the network's structure. We detail the key components of this framework, including the quantum state initialization, self-organization algorithms, and control mechanisms that govern network evolution. The paper concludes with a detailed discussion of the theoretical foundation, experimental validation, and future research directions of this innovative approach.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks via Adaptive Weight Decay with Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Neural networks have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, yet they suffer from significant challenges, notably catastrophic forgetting and overfitting. These issues limit their ability to effectively generalize across diverse tasks and maintain performance over time. This paper introduces a novel approach to mitigate these problems through adaptive weight decay, combined with Bayesian optimization. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the weight decay rate, rather than using a fixed value, based on the network's learning progress. A Bayesian optimization framework is then employed to determine the optimal decay rate for each parameter, creating a feedback loop for continuous refinement. The proposed method improves robustness and generalization performance, offering a self-correcting mechanism for neural networks. The theoretical underpinnings of this approach are presented, focusing on the impact of weight decay on gradient descent and the optimization strategy used to determine the optimal decay rate. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of simulations, showcasing its ability to reduce catastrophic forgetting and overfitting.

title: Distributed Quantum Machine Learning Fault-Tolerant Error Correction Codes
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to fault-tolerant error correction coding specifically designed for distributed quantum machine learning (DQLM) environments. The core challenge in DQLM lies in preserving the delicate quantum states – superposition and entanglement – necessary for quantum algorithms, while simultaneously mitigating the detrimental effects of noise and decoherence inherent in distributed quantum computation. Existing quantum error correction techniques often require significant overhead and complex control, making them less suitable for the dynamic and resource-constrained nature of DQLM. We introduce a coding scheme predicated on leveraging quantum entanglement and parallel processing capabilities of distributed quantum computers. This scheme provides real-time error correction and recovery, enhancing the accuracy and reliability of machine learning algorithms. The key contribution is a tailored error correction strategy that directly addresses the unique vulnerabilities of DQLM, offering a pathway towards practical and robust quantum machine learning. We formalize the error correction process with mathematical notation, outlining the encoding, decoding, and correction operations. The proposed framework demonstrates significant potential for improving the performance and scalability of DQLM.

abstract: Adaptive Topology-Constraint Computation is a novel computational method that leverages self-adaptive topology constraints to enhance efficiency. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional constraint-based methods by offering a more flexible and efficient solution. The key contribution lies in the implementation of a self-optimizing constraint adjustment process that significantly reduces the number of iterations required for achieving a target solution. title: Predictive Programming Based on Biological Neuron Simulation
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to programming by leveraging the underlying mechanisms of biological neurons. The core idea is to simulate the behavior of neurons to generate programs with inherent robustness and adaptability. We propose a framework that creates highly detailed neuron models and utilizes them to produce code. This process mimics the synaptic connections and signal transmission within biological neurons, effectively translating neural activity into executable programs. The significance of this work lies in exploring a fundamentally new paradigm for programming, inspired by the complex and efficient processing capabilities of the human brain. The generated programs exhibit characteristics mirroring biological neural networks, such as resilience to noise and the ability to adapt to changing environments. This research outlines the theoretical foundations, the proposed simulation methodology, and discusses the potential implications of this approach for developing future computing paradigms. ---

title: A High-Throughput Memory Compression Architecture for Real-Time 3D Visual Tracking and Quantification on Edge Devices
abstract: The deployment of real-time three-dimensional (3D) visual perception, continuous spatial sensing, and graphics-intensive multimedia applications on embedded edge devices introduces substantial runtime memory pressure. During execution, these workloads continuously generate small-granularity memory pages, including image buffers, depth maps, rendering caches, intermediate feature tensors, and media buffers. To reduce memory footprint while preserving low processing overhead, this paper proposes a sequence-aware cascaded compression framework for runtime memory pages generated by visual and multimedia workloads. Instead of following the traditional restore-then-recompress path, the proposed framework directly reuses the intermediate sequence representation produced by LZ4. It parses LZ4 sequences into literal and structured stream sequences and applies stream-specific entropy coding using Huffman and Finite State Entropy (FSE) coding. By avoiding full-page restoration and repeated redundancy analysis, the framework preserves lossless reconstruction semantics while reducing compression overhead. Experimental results on real-world runtime memory pages show that the proposed framework reduces compression processing time by 42.10% on average and by up to 52.22%. It also reduces Central Processing Unit (CPU) time by 20.28% on average and peak memory usage by 29.92% on average. Additional validation on a RISC-V edge platform shows that the compression processing time is reduced by up to 64.36%. A 16 MB point-cloud memory sample derived from 3D scan data further shows a 33.16% reduction in compression time. Functional tests on more than 200K mixed-entropy memory pages demonstrate 100% lossless reconstruction and successful detection of corrupted compressed streams.

title: PASTEL: Panoramic Alignment for Monocular 4D Scene Reconstruction
abstract: Reconstructing 4D scenes from casually captured monocular video is vital for applications in virtual reality (VR) and embodied AI. Recent advances in 4D reconstruction and novel view synthesis have substantially propelled this capability. However, existing reconstruction methods generally cannot recover regions beyond visible camera limits. Consequently, we introduce a new paradigm that achieves 4D scene synthesis by combining visible-region reconstruction from monocular input with invisible-region generation beyond observable camera boundaries. We present Panoramic Alignment for Strategic Exploitation of Generative Priors (PASTEL). Specifically, PASTEL proposes panoramic scene alignment, a novel representation that reformulates the intractable 3D "invisible region" exploration into a tractable 2D directional trajectory planning. This is achieved by reducing the viewpoint planning from 6-DoF search to a 2D directional search with explicit visibility boundaries. By operating within this panoramic space, our method strategically identifies camera trajectories that maximize exploration beyond observable boundaries while minimizing viewpoint deviation. Experimental results show that PASTEL can not only extrapolate plausible scene content beyond the observable boundaries of input monocular videos, but also substantially boost monocular 4D reconstruction performance. PASTEL outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method by 0.9dB in full-image PSNR on the DyCheck IPhone dataset.

title: Prompt Engineering: Techniques, Empirical Study, and Future Directions
abstract: Prompt engineering — the practice of deliberately crafting input instructions to guide large language model (LLM) behavior — has emerged as a critical competency in applied artificial intelligence. This paper provides a comprehensive treatment of the field, combining a structured literature review with an original empirical study. In the empirical component, three core prompting techniques — zero-shot prompting, few shot prompting, and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting — were systematically tested against Claude Sonnet (claude-sonnet-4-20250514) across three task categories: mathematical reasoning, logical syllogism evaluation, and Python code generation. Results demonstrate that chain-of-thought prompting consistently produces the most complete, accurate, and auditable outputs, while zero-shot prompting — despite its efficiency — is prone to logical errors in tasks requiring formal reasoning. Few-shot prompting occupies a productive middle ground, delivering structured accuracy with moderate token overhead. Beyond empirical findings, the paper surveys major theoretical frameworks, real-world applications, open challenges including prompt injection and hallucination, and future research directions encompassing automatic prompt optimization, multimodal prompting, and agent-based systems. This paper is intended to serve as both a technical reference and a portfolio demonstration of applied AI research methodology. Keywords: prompt engineering, large language models, zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, empirical study, Claude Sonnet, AI reasoning, prompt injection, LLM evaluation

title: Algorithm Security Proof based on Quantum Noise
abstract: Traditional algorithm security proofs heavily rely on computational complexity assumptions, which are increasingly vulnerable in the face of quantum computing. This paper introduces a novel approach to algorithm security proofing based on quantum noise. The core idea is to leverage the inherent statistical properties of quantum noise to construct a security model and formally verify the security of algorithms. This method circumvents the dependence on intractable computational assumptions, offering a potentially robust security framework for future computing paradigms. We present a formal model incorporating noise characteristics and demonstrate its applicability through a theoretical analysis, highlighting the potential of this approach to address the challenges posed by quantum computing threats. The proposed method aims to provide a more resilient approach to algorithm security assurance.

title: Quantum-Inspired Cryptographic Key Exchange using Graph-Based Routing
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cryptographic key exchange protocol leveraging concepts inspired by quantum mechanics, specifically superposition and probabilistic exploration, through a graph-based routing mechanism. Traditional key exchange protocols often rely on computationally intensive mathematical problems, making them vulnerable to advancements in computing power, including quantum computers. Our approach aims to mitigate this vulnerability by employing a graph structure to represent potential communication partners and utilizing a probabilistic routing algorithm that mimics the superposition principle. This allows for the simultaneous evaluation of multiple routing paths, dramatically increasing the computational complexity for an attacker while simultaneously reducing latency. The core of the system is a dynamically constructed graph where nodes represent potential key exchange partners and edges represent communication channels with associated security scores calculated probabilistically. The algorithm then iteratively explores this graph, utilizing a 'superposition' effect to consider multiple paths concurrently. The path with the highest security score is selected, ensuring robust key exchange. This method offers a potentially more resilient key exchange solution against both classical and future quantum attacks. The performance of this approach is evaluated through theoretical analysis and the design of a simplified prototype, demonstrating its potential for enhanced security and efficiency.

title: 基于非线性动力学建模的程序行为预测
abstract: This paper explores the application of nonlinear dynamics modeling to predict program behavior within complex environments. Traditional approaches to program analysis often rely on linear approximations or simplified models, which can fail to capture the intricate and emergent behaviors that arise from non-linear interactions. This research posits that program behavior can be effectively modeled as a nonlinear dynamical system, allowing for a more accurate and robust prediction of program outcomes. The core of this work lies in utilizing nonlinear dynamics theory – including concepts like phase space analysis, Lyapunov exponents, and Poincaré sections – to analyze and forecast program behavior. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach, highlighting its ability to improve program robustness and adaptability in dynamic scenarios. The presented methodology offers a new perspective on program analysis, moving beyond linear models to embrace the inherent complexity of real-world program execution. The key contributions of this research include a formal framework for translating program logic into a dynamical system representation, and a methodology for extracting predictive insights from the resulting models. This approach holds promise for applications in areas such as software verification, automated testing, and adaptive program design.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Clustering Algorithms for Big Data
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum algorithms to enhance clustering performance on big data. Traditional clustering algorithms often struggle with the computational complexity associated with large datasets and intricate data distributions. We propose and analyze the implementation of quantum k-means and quantum hierarchical clustering algorithms, leveraging quantum superposition and entanglement to potentially achieve significant speedups. The theoretical framework outlines the core concepts and mathematical formulations of these algorithms. We explore the potential for quantum algorithms to address the limitations of classical approaches, particularly in scenarios involving high-dimensional data and complex clusters. The research focuses on the algorithmic design, examining the key steps involved in transforming classical clustering problems into quantum computations. This work contributes to the emerging field of quantum data mining and provides a foundational understanding of how quantum computing can revolutionize data analysis tasks. The primary focus is on the theoretical aspects of quantum clustering and does not include experimental validation.

title: Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks for Synthetic Data Augmentation
abstract: This paper explores the application of Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (QGANs) for synthetic data augmentation, aiming to surpass the limitations of classical Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We investigate the potential of utilizing quantum circuits to implement the generator and discriminator components of a GAN, capitalizing on quantum phenomena like superposition and interference to enhance the data generation process. Our research demonstrates that QGANs, in principle, can produce synthetic data with improved quality and diversity, particularly when dealing with complex and high-dimensional datasets. We present a theoretical framework and analysis, highlighting the core claim that QGANs offer a promising avenue for generating more realistic and varied synthetic data. The novelty of this work lies in the exploration of quantum-enhanced GANs for data augmentation, a field with significant potential for advancing machine learning applications. The core mechanism focuses on harnessing quantum mechanics to refine the generative process.

title: Emergent Information Encoding via Quantum Phase Transitions
abstract: Quantum phase transitions represent a profound shift in the behavior of matter, offering the potential for novel information processing paradigms. This paper explores the application of quantum phase transitions to encode and decode information within complex, multi-layered systems, leveraging quantum coherence for robust and efficient data storage and retrieval. We investigate a novel quantum algorithm designed to exploit multiple quantum phases to create a layered structure that enables information transfer and manipulation. The core claim is that this approach can overcome limitations of classical information encoding, offering a fundamentally new pathway for data storage and processing. We detail the design of the algorithm, its potential applications, and preliminary results demonstrating the feasibility of this emergent information encoding method.

title: Quantum State Generation via Adaptive Entanglement
abstract: Quantum state generation is a crucial cornerstone of quantum information processing, particularly in quantum communication and quantum computing. Current approaches often rely on pre-defined entanglement schemes, limiting their adaptability to complex and dynamic environments. This paper introduces a novel quantum state generation algorithm, termed "Adaptive Entanglement Generation," that dynamically adjusts the strength and pattern of entanglement based on input data. The core mechanism involves a quantum environment simulator that iteratively adjusts the entanglement parameters, enabling a far more flexible and powerful generation process than conventional methods. This advancement addresses the limitations of static entanglement schemes, offering a significant step toward more efficient and practical quantum technologies. The algorithm demonstrates its efficacy through simulated experiments, showcasing enhanced entanglement fidelity and improved communication protocols.

abstract: Quantum Geometry Entropy – Based on Quantum Entanglement for Geometric Assessment This paper explores the application of quantum entanglement to the evaluation of geometric structures, offering a novel approach to quantifying entropy and facilitating optimization. Traditional geometric assessment methods rely on classical computation, while this algorithm utilizes quantum entanglement to achieve enhanced accuracy. The research introduces a "Quantum Geometry Entropy Assessment Module" designed to quantify geometric entropy through entanglement and subsequently optimize the resulting structure. This work presents a framework for evaluating geometric properties with a fundamentally different approach, potentially revolutionizing geometric analysis and optimization.

title: Adaptive Neural Symbolic Representation Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to neural-symbolic representation learning that addresses the limitations of existing hybrid systems in dynamically adapting to data complexity and uncertainty. The core idea is to develop a recurrent neural network architecture where the symbolic representation itself is not static but evolves through a differentiable process, guided by a "contextual uncertainty" module. This module learns to adjust the granularity of the symbolic representation – shifting between abstract concepts and concrete instances – based on the inherent ambiguity or noise present in the input data. The proposed system offers a flexible and robust framework for reasoning with imperfect information, potentially leading to improved performance in tasks requiring both symbolic knowledge and adaptive learning. The key innovation lies in the continuous, uncertainty-driven refinement of the symbolic representation, moving beyond fixed symbolic structures. The system's architecture and training procedure are presented, and preliminary results are discussed, demonstrating its ability to handle varying levels of data complexity and uncertainty. We aim to provide a foundation for more sophisticated neural-symbolic systems capable of truly understanding and reasoning about the world. ---

title: Formal Verification of Quantum Circuit Optimization Algorithms
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is crucial for realizing the full potential of quantum computing. However, the inherent complexity of quantum circuits and the potential for errors introduce significant challenges in ensuring the correctness and efficiency of optimization algorithms. This paper proposes a novel approach to formally verify quantum circuit optimization algorithms. We translate these algorithms into formal specification languages and leverage model checking and theorem proving techniques to rigorously demonstrate that the algorithms meet their intended objectives – primarily minimizing circuit complexity – without introducing unintended side effects. The core contribution lies in applying formal verification methodologies to this largely unexplored area, offering a path towards building trust and confidence in quantum optimization strategies. The presented framework provides a systematic method for ensuring the reliability of quantum circuits, a critical step towards practical quantum computation. The verification process relies on defining the desired behavior as a set of logical properties and then employing automated tools to check whether the optimized circuit satisfies these properties. This approach addresses the fundamental need for rigorous assurance in quantum systems, moving beyond empirical validation and towards mathematically proven correctness.

title: Probability Logic and Quantum Entanglement: A Unified Theory
abstract: This paper explores the convergence of probability logic and quantum entanglement, proposing a novel quantum computing paradigm that leverages probability logic as the fundamental description of quantum entanglement and integrates quantum entanglement's inherent properties to enhance computational capabilities. We investigate a framework where probability logic provides the underlying dynamics of entanglement, allowing for probabilistic quantum computation. The core mechanism involves constructing a quantum computation system where the evolution of quantum states is governed by probability logic rules, intrinsically linked to the entanglement dynamics. This approach aims to surpass the limitations of traditional quantum computing by introducing a more flexible and efficient approach to quantum data processing. The resulting framework offers a potential pathway toward significantly enhanced quantum computational performance and data handling capabilities.

title: Dynamic Topology for Quantum State Propagation
abstract: Quantum state propagation, the precise manipulation of quantum states across a network, is a critical challenge in quantum information processing. Traditional approaches often rely on static topologies, limiting control and analysis capabilities. This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology, designed to adapt to the evolving state of quantum systems, thereby enhancing fidelity and enabling new functionalities. We propose a self-organizing topology that dynamically adjusts connections based on the quantum state, fostering precise state propagation. The core mechanism leverages a feedback loop that optimizes the network's structure to minimize errors and maximize state preservation. This work represents a significant advancement in quantum state propagation, offering a more adaptable and powerful framework for quantum experimentation and control.

title: Adaptive Bayesian Networks for Online Anomaly Detection
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to online anomaly detection utilizing adaptive Bayesian Networks (ABNs). Traditional Bayesian Networks (BNs) often fail to effectively handle the dynamic nature of real-world data streams, leading to inaccurate anomaly detection. Our approach overcomes this limitation by dynamically updating the conditional probability tables within a BN using a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm. The RL agent is guided by anomaly signals, allowing the network to continuously learn and adapt to the evolving underlying data distribution. We define a formal framework for this adaptive BN, outlining the key components and their interactions. The core concept involves constructing a BN where node parameters, specifically the conditional probabilities, are continuously refined. This creates a self-adapting system capable of identifying deviations from the learned "normal" behavior. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and provide a detailed description of the algorithm. The resulting adaptive system offers improved responsiveness and accuracy compared to static BNs in online anomaly detection scenarios. The system's ability to learn and adjust its internal parameters based on incoming data makes it particularly well-suited for environments where the normal behavior is not stationary. The primary contribution lies in the synergistic combination of Bayesian inference and reinforcement learning, providing a robust and adaptable solution for real-time anomaly detection.

title: Efficacy Evaluation and Optimization of RAG Knowledge Bases in the Oil and Gas Industry Using an LLM-as-a-Judge Mechanism
abstract: The increasing adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in the oil and gas industry has created a growing need for systematic evaluation of domain-specific knowledge bases, particularly with respect to retrieval failures, numerical and entity inconsistencies, knowledge timeliness, and unsupported generation. This study presents a domain-adapted evaluation and optimization framework for industrial RAG knowledge bases based on an LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm. The framework organizes evaluation into four dimensions—Data, Retrieval, Generation, and Utility (DAAE)—and combines deterministic metrics with LLM-based semantic assessment. A two-tier evaluation procedure combines retrieval-based screening with fine-grained LLM judging while retaining retrieval failures in end-to-end evaluation statistics. Rather than introducing new retrieval or generation algorithms, the framework integrates established RAG techniques with evaluation criteria motivated by oil-and-gas knowledge characteristics, including domain-entity and numerical consistency, temporal validity, chunk-level semantic integrity, and controlled abstention. Evaluation results are mapped to corresponding optimization actions across the data, retrieval, and generation layers, including semantic-aware chunking, metadata augmentation, hybrid sparse–dense retrieval, Cross-Encoder reranking, and structured evidence-grounded prompting. The framework was evaluated using the Intelligent Knowledge Base for Natural Gas Economic Research and an expert-annotated benchmark comprising 150 domain questions. In the industrial before–after comparison, Retrieval Hit@5 increased from 58.0% (87/150) to 89.3% (134/150), Context Precision increased from 0.64 to 0.88, and Faithfulness increased from 0.65 to 0.94. These values are reported as system-level point estimates rather than as component-wise causal effects. The results demonstrate the practical value of evaluation-guided optimization for improving the reliability of domain-specific RAG systems in natural-gas economic research and provide an industrial case for systematic RAG assessment and iterative optimization in the energy sector.

title: SLA-Safe Energy Control for AI-Native NG-RAN Using Stability-Aware Constrained PPO
abstract: One important AI-for-RAN use case is energy saving, in which radio resources and cell energy modes must be dynamically controlled without violating user quality-of-service (QoS) or service-level agreement (SLA) requirements. However, aggressive sleep-state or deactivation decisions may reduce energy consumption at the cost of throughput degradation, delay increase, SLA violations, and unstable mode switching, especially under time-varying and bursty traffic conditions. This paper proposes a stability-aware constrained reinforcement learning framework for SLA-safe energy control in 5G NG-RAN. The problem is formulated as a constrained Markov decision process in which an AI-native controller selects closed-loop energy-saving actions based on cell load, queue status, active-user information, current energy mode, and SLA-related indicators. The proposed framework uses constrained proximal policy optimization with adaptive Lagrangian penalties to account for throughput, delay, and SLA constraints. To improve operation under traffic distribution shift, the controller is trained using mixed nominal and stress traffic regimes, while a switching-stability penalty is introduced to reduce oscillatory transitions between active and low-power modes. Simulation results in a seven-cell NG-RAN environment show that the proposed controller reduces energy consumption by approximately 41.4% under nominal traffic, 10.5% under stress traffic, and 22.9% under unseen-stress traffic relative to the Always-On baseline. Under stress and unseen-stress traffic, the controller preserves zero SLA violation and zero throughput loss, indicating service-preserving operation under challenging conditions. The proposed method also reduces switching activity compared with basic threshold-based energy saving.

title: Dynamic Memory Allocation via Reservoir Computing with Reservoir Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to dynamic memory allocation using Reservoir Neural Networks (RNNs). The core idea is to harness the inherent temporal dynamics of RNNs to effectively manage memory resources without the need for traditional, explicit allocation schemes. We demonstrate that by training an RNN reservoir, the network learns to map input signals directly to desired output states, effectively storing and retrieving information. Crucially, the size and connectivity of the reservoir can be dynamically adjusted based on the demands of the application, leading to a highly adaptive and efficient memory allocation system. This approach avoids the overhead associated with traditional memory management techniques, offering potential improvements in performance and resource utilization. The key innovation lies in treating memory allocation as a learning problem for the RNN, allowing it to optimize its internal state for specific tasks. The theoretical framework and underlying mechanisms are presented, outlining the potential for widespread application in diverse scenarios requiring adaptive memory management. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential limitations.

title: QSafety QAE: Quantum amplitude estimation tools for safety probability models
abstract: Independently authored tools for comparing classical Monte Carlo and ideal maximum-likelihood quantum amplitude estimation in safety and reliability probability models. The repository also contains selected uncertainty, strong-classical-baseline, schedule, and finite-table oracle research scripts. This is a code-only software archive, not a complete manuscript data archive or a claim of end-to-end quantum advantage. The PyPI wheel provides the core qsafety library; research scripts are available from the tagged repository.

title: Adaptive Probability Distribution Machine Learning Model
abstract: This paper explores the design of a novel machine learning model leveraging adaptive probability distribution techniques. The core claim is that a dynamically adjusting parameter and distribution set, driven by training data, will enhance model generalization and robustness. Traditional machine learning models often suffer from fixed parameter sets, limiting their ability to adapt to evolving data. This paper proposes a mechanism to optimize model parameters through a dynamic adjustment process, resulting in improved performance. The model's foundation rests on the concept of continuously refining its probability distribution based on observed data, thereby fostering better adaptability.

abstract: The field-adaptive generalization model aims to address the limitations of traditional generalized models by dynamically adjusting model parameters based on data distribution. The model's effectiveness is predicated on an iterative refinement process, continually adjusting parameters to optimally represent the target data distribution. This represents a significant advancement in model optimization, offering a more robust and adaptable solution compared to static parameter tuning methods. The model's core mechanism hinges on a feedback loop that analyzes data distributions during training, adjusting parameters to achieve a better representation of the underlying data patterns. This iterative adjustment process is crucial for achieving high performance in various scenarios.

This work demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in model accuracy and robustness.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state generation algorithm based on adaptive topology. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results, illustrating its capability to generate complex and controllable quantum states.

title: Quantum Simulation via Probabilistic Field Theory: A Novel Approach to Physical Validation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to physical validation utilizing probabilistic field theory and quantum simulation. Traditional quantum simulation often demands substantial computational resources, increasing experimental costs. We propose a system that leverages probabilistic field theory to rigorously validate physical models, particularly in the context of quantum systems. The core mechanism centers around a combined probabilistic field theory and quantum simulation framework, designed to drastically reduce computational complexity while simultaneously enhancing simulation efficiency. This approach offers a promising pathway to significantly lower the cost and time associated with quantum system research. The paper details the system architecture, the theoretical underpinnings of the probabilistic field theory, and a preliminary evaluation of its efficacy in validating a specific physical model.

title: Symbolic Simulation of Quantum Circuits with Tensor Networks
abstract: The accurate simulation of quantum circuits remains a significant challenge due to the exponential scaling of computational resources with circuit size. This work explores the application of tensor network methods, specifically Matrix Product States (MPS), to provide a scalable approach for simulating quantum circuits. We demonstrate how tensor networks can efficiently represent and manipulate the states of quantum circuits, reducing the computational burden associated with traditional methods. The core claim of this research is that tensor networks offer a viable path to accurately simulating larger and more complex quantum systems. This research introduces a novel framework for symbolic simulation, leveraging the power of tensor network representations to overcome the limitations of conventional simulation techniques. The effectiveness of this approach is illustrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual examples.

title: Multi-Modal Active Learning with Causal Inference
abstract: Active learning (AL) aims to reduce annotation costs by strategically selecting the most informative samples for labeling. Traditional AL methods often rely on uncertainty sampling or query-by-committee approaches, which may not effectively capture the underlying dependencies between different data modalities. This paper introduces a novel approach to multi-modal active learning that leverages causal inference to identify samples with the highest potential to reduce model uncertainty. We hypothesize that understanding the causal relationships between modalities can guide the selection process, leading to improved learning efficiency and model accuracy. Our framework utilizes causal graphs and Bayesian networks to model the dependencies between modalities, quantifying the impact of labeling a particular sample on reducing uncertainty. Specifically, we define the core claim as: *In multi-modal active learning, causal inference can be used to identify the most informative samples, thereby improving learning efficiency and model accuracy.* The core mechanism involves combining causal graphs and Bayesian networks to analyze relationships between modalities and determine samples that maximally reduce model uncertainty. This work represents a new direction in AL by integrating causal reasoning, enhancing the intelligence and effectiveness of multi-modal learning systems.

title: Non-Linear Neural Networks: Adaptive Parameter Adjustment
abstract: Non-linear neural networks have emerged as a powerful tool for tackling complex data and tasks, offering increased flexibility and the potential for superior performance compared to traditional linear models. This paper introduces a novel approach to non-linear neural networks, termed "Adaptive Parameter Adjustment" (APA). APA leverages a dynamic parameter adjustment strategy, dynamically adjusting the network's internal parameters to optimize model performance across a range of input complexities. The core mechanism involves a sophisticated self-learning algorithm that continuously monitors and adjusts the network's weights and biases, ensuring a robust and adaptable representation. This paper details the methodology, presents experimental results demonstrating significant performance improvements, and concludes with a discussion of the advantages and potential applications of this approach.

The system learns to optimize the network's structure based on task feedback, resulting in a self-organizing network capable of adapting to varying demands. The key contribution lies in the integration of reinforcement learning with a dynamic topology, providing a framework for creating more efficient and robust neural networks. The theoretical framework presented here outlines a methodology for building adaptive neural networks, offering a promising direction for future research in neural network design and optimization.

title: Dynamic Topologically-Dependent Graph Optimization Algorithm (DTDOA)
abstract: This paper introduces the Dynamic Topologically-Dependent Graph Optimization Algorithm (DTDOA), a novel approach to optimization problems where the underlying dependency graph is subject to continuous changes. Existing graph optimization algorithms often struggle with this dynamic nature, leading to performance degradation. DTDOA addresses this limitation by leveraging reinforcement learning to dynamically adapt to evolving topological structures. The algorithm constructs a state representation capturing the current topological information and employs an action space to adjust the weights and priorities within the dependency graph. The core claim is that a reinforcement learning-based system can learn and adapt to changing topologies in real-time, minimizing performance loss. The method's novelty lies in its direct application of reinforcement learning to the dynamic topology problem, moving beyond static dependency graphs or pre-defined optimization strategies. This approach promises significant improvements in scenarios where the system's operational environment is characterized by frequent topological alterations.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Artistic Image Classification in Visual IoT Sensor Networks
abstract: Visual Internet-of-Things (IoT) cameras and institution-controlled edge gateways increasingly collect artwork images in museums, galleries, and heritage sites. Centralizing these images can expose collection contents, exhibition layouts, and contextual information. This paper proposes FedArtSense, a privacy-preserving federated learning framework for artistic style and medium classification. FedArtSense combines discrepancy-adaptive dual-space prototype alignment, client-level differential privacy for model and prototype releases, and importance-aware shared sparsification compatible with secure aggregation. Experiments on WikiArt, ArtBench-10, and a seven-class Behance Artistic Media subset use emulated non-IID client partitions, persistent acquisition shifts, constrained uplinks, and client dropout. Under the default client-level target (ϵ,δ)=(6,10−5), FedArtSense obtains accuracies of 64.2%, 81.2%, and 75.3%, respectively, while reducing cumulative WikiArt uplink traffic to 11.5 GiB. The results support FedArtSense as a privacy–utility–communication trade-off for gateway-assisted artistic image classification; retrieval, detection, aesthetic prediction, and direct battery-powered camera training are outside the evaluated scope.

title: Learning as Graph Traversal
abstract: Large text corpora rarely arrive with the structure a reader needs to navigate them. We present an end-to-end system that induces navigable trails through a flat collection of 323,552 quizbowl questions — short academic quiz texts, each with a canonical answer but no authored links — and serves them to learners through a deployed, multimodal study platform. An offline pipeline segments each question into sentences, embeds them with an instruction-tuned encoder, and clusters each answer’s sentences into concept nodes. Rather than linking concepts by co-occurrence, we order them with optimal leaf ordering (OLO) over their embedding hierarchy, producing, for each subject and difficulty level, a single guided tour that minimizes the total dissimilarity between consecutive concepts. Each tour is at once the navigable structure and the first-exposure sequence; an FSRS-7 spaced-repetition scheduler then governs revisitation at concept granularity. The platform scaffolds each encounter along a five-level ladder of fading support, from highlighted reading with synchronized audio to audio-only recall. The pipeline and platform are the artifacts. A sampled transition audit finds 96% of trail steps land on a related concept; a formative usage observation shows recall accuracy rising with repeated spaced encounters. Establishing pedagogical efficacy remains future work.

title: Differentiable Horn Programs: A Constructive Expressivity Theorem for Latent Rule Operators
abstract: We introduce \textsc{LatentGamma}, a differentiable operator on the unit cube $[0,1]^M$ designed as a smooth surrogate of Tarski's immediate consequence operator $\TP$ associated with a definite Horn program $P$ on $M$ atoms. The operator is built as a five-stage composition combining sigmoidal gating, softmax routing, and a residual update that enforces monotonicity by construction. We establish four theoretical results. First, the iterated sequence is coordinate-wise non-decreasing and bounded by $\ind$, hence converges to a fixed point of \textsc{LatentGamma}; the operator itself is lattice-monotone on $[0,1]^M$. Second, our \emph{constructive expressivity theorem} shows that for every definite Horn program $P$ there exists a closed-form parameter assignment $θ^*(P)$ and an explicit time bound $T_{\max}(P)$ such that the iterated sequence \emph{exactly} reproduces $\TPinf(F_0)$ for every initial fact set $F_0$ throughout the window $[D(P, F_0), T_{\max}(P)]$, where $D(P, F_0) \leq M$ is the derivation depth. The window $T_{\max}$ is large in practice ($\geq 10^5$ for sparse programs) and reflects the finite-time nature of computation by smooth sigmoidal gates. Third, the oracle is robust to Gaussian noise on its body and head logits, with explicit non-asymptotic bounds. Fourth, we prove a matching information-theoretic lower bound on the parameter count. We provide a complete numerical validation on programs ranging from $M = 33$ to $M = 504$ atoms: oracle accuracy reaches $1.0000$ on $2000$ test cases with zero false-positive and false-negative rates, and the empirical noise tolerance $σ_{\max}$ scales precisely as the union bound $RM \cdot Φ(-10/σ_η)$ predicts.

title: Flawed but Memorable: Student Critical Reception of Interest-Personalized GenAI Analogies in Computing Education
abstract: Motivation: Undergraduate computing students increasingly turn to generative AI (GenAI) tools to understand abstract concepts through analogies. Analogies compare an unfamiliar concept to something familiar, but judging whether the comparison holds requires knowledge of both. GenAI may also embed assumptions about who the learner is. GenAI education research centers on output correctness, leaving students' critical reception of analogies largely unexamined. Method: We investigate how students evaluate the accuracy, appropriateness, and assumptions in GenAI-generated analogies, and their perceptions of interest-personalized versus generic technical explanations. Ten students with CS2 experience participated in a pre-survey, a think-aloud task with linked-list and recursion explanations, and a semi-structured interview grounded in the Paul-Elder framework. They judged accuracy, clarity, engagement, and trust separately. Results: Most participants described interest-personalized analogies as more engaging or memorable than generic technical explanations, while trust was mixed. Some trusted the tailored analogies more; others scrutinized them more closely or distrusted the tailoring. Participants with deep source-domain knowledge identified structural flaws requiring that knowledge to recognize. Because personalization and explanation format differed together, these findings do not isolate an effect of personalization alone. Implications: A familiar source flips the student's role. On the concept they are still learners, but on the familiar source they are the expert, and that is the position from which an analogy can be judged. We call this two-sided analogy auditing. GenAI systems should ask what students know, not just what interests them, and treat a flawed analogy as something to inspect and fix rather than accept.

title: Codes of length 18 over Non-Abelian Groups
abstract: Consider the semisimple group algebra F𝒢, where F is a finite field and 𝒢 is a non-abelian group of order 18. In this paper, we derive both linear and non-linear primitive idempotents by utilizing the character theory of 𝒢, and these idempotents are used to construct a family of group codes. Furthermore, we determine fundamental parameters of these group codes.

title: Dynamic Programming with Adaptive State Abstraction
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to dynamic programming (DP) that addresses the inherent limitations of traditional DP methods, specifically their exponential state space growth. The core idea is to integrate adaptive state abstraction techniques directly into the DP process. Instead of relying on a fixed, exhaustive state space representation, the proposed method dynamically learns and applies state abstraction strategies based on observed problem data patterns. This is achieved through a learned 'summarization' layer, which effectively reduces the state space complexity, enabling the application of DP to significantly larger and more intricate problems. The method's key contribution lies in the dynamic and adaptive nature of state abstraction, moving beyond static abstraction techniques. The performance of this approach is demonstrated conceptually, focusing on the design principles and the potential for future implementations. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the key components and their interactions. The paper concludes with a discussion on future research directions and potential applications.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Memory Storage (QED-DMS)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed memory storage system, termed Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Memory Storage (QED-DMS), which leverages quantum entanglement to achieve unprecedented storage capacity and fidelity. The core concept involves creating multiple entangled qubit collections and strategically manipulating these collections to encode and store information across distributed nodes. Unlike classical distributed storage systems reliant on bandwidth-limited information transfer, QED-DMS exploits the non-local nature of quantum entanglement to overcome physical constraints, offering significantly higher storage density and data access rates. The system's architecture allows for efficient information retrieval and updates via entanglement-mediated communication. We present a theoretical framework outlining the system's operation, focusing on the key aspects of entanglement distribution, state manipulation, and information encoding. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the potential for QED-DMS to surpass the limitations of conventional storage technologies. The system's performance is characterized by high storage fidelity and robust data access, driven by the inherent properties of quantum entanglement. Further research and development are required to realize the full potential of QED-DMS, potentially through advancements in quantum memory technology and entanglement generation techniques. ---

title: 基于量子纠缠的密钥协商协议
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum key agreement protocol leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. Current quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols often rely on quantum superposition states, introducing potential vulnerabilities. This protocol aims to enhance security by exploiting the inherent correlations provided by quantum entanglement. We detail the protocol's architecture, focusing on the entanglement distribution phase, the key distillation phase, and the key agreement phase. The protocol incorporates elements of quantum cryptography to ensure secure key encryption and decryption. The core claim is that this entanglement-based approach offers a superior level of security compared to superposition-based protocols. Mathematical formulations are presented to illustrate key aspects of the protocol, including the probability of successful key agreement and the security assumptions. The protocol's design addresses potential threats by fundamentally relying on the non-classical correlations established through entanglement. This approach represents a significant step towards more robust and secure quantum key distribution.

title: Dynamic Program Synthesis via Evolutionary Algorithms and Formal Specification Languages
abstract: This research investigates a novel approach to program synthesis – dynamic program synthesis – leveraging the strengths of evolutionary algorithms and formal specification languages. The core idea is to automate the process of generating executable code directly from formally defined requirements. Traditional program synthesis techniques often struggle with complexity and scalability. This work proposes a framework where an evolutionary algorithm iteratively refines code solutions, guided by a formal specification language that provides precise and unambiguous requirements. The algorithm explores the solution space effectively, and the formal language ensures that generated code always adheres to the intended design. The approach demonstrates the potential for automating complex program generation tasks, addressing a significant challenge in software engineering. We define the core concepts, the encoding mechanism, and the algorithm design, highlighting the synergy between these elements. The key contribution lies in the systematic integration of evolutionary optimization with rigorous formal specification, offering a new paradigm for automated code generation. The results presented showcase the feasibility and effectiveness of this combined approach.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) is a cornerstone of artificial intelligence, aiming to develop systems capable of mechanically deriving mathematical theorems. Traditional ATP systems rely heavily on handcrafted heuristics and logical inference rules, often requiring significant human intervention. This research explores the application of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to automate theorem proving. The core idea involves training a DRL agent to navigate the complex space of logical manipulations, learning optimal strategies for theorem proving through trial and error. The system is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) where the agent's actions are logical inferences, the state represents the current theorem and proof context, and the reward function guides the agent towards successful proof completion. We hypothesize that DRL's capacity to learn intricate patterns and representations from raw data can overcome the limitations of traditional ATP systems, potentially leading to more robust and efficient automated reasoning. This paper details the design of the DRL-based ATP system, focusing on the formulation of the MDP, the choice of the DRL architecture, and the reward function design. Preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and highlight the potential for future advancements.

title: Distributed Learning with Federated Byzantine Fault Tolerance (FBT)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed learning that leverages the principles of Federated Byzantine Fault Tolerance (FBT) to achieve robustness and scalability against malicious actors. Traditional federated learning systems are vulnerable to attacks where adversaries can manipulate the global model by injecting poisoned updates. Our method integrates FBT protocols, originally designed for blockchain consensus, into the distributed learning framework. This allows nodes to reach agreement on model updates even when some nodes are compromised and actively attempting to disrupt the learning process. We demonstrate that this combination provides a significant improvement in security and reliability compared to standard federated learning, offering a pathway to secure and trustworthy distributed model training. The core claim of this work is that robust and scalable distributed learning in the presence of malicious actors is a significant challenge, and our proposed solution directly addresses this issue.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Causal Inference with Bayesian Networks and Markov Chain Monte Carlo
abstract: This paper proposes a novel probabilistic programming language designed to streamline the process of causal inference. The core of the language is its seamless integration of Bayesian Networks and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, offering a unified framework for modeling and reasoning about uncertainty within causal relationships. The language provides built-in support for defining causal models, executing Bayesian inference, and sampling from posterior distributions, effectively addressing challenges such as confounding and selection bias. Unlike existing approaches that often require specialized software or manual implementation of complex algorithms, this language aims to democratize causal inference by providing a more accessible and intuitive tool for researchers. The key innovation lies in automating the intricate steps involved in causal modeling, allowing users to focus on the underlying causal questions rather than the technical details of the inference process. This facilitates more robust and reliable causal discovery and inference.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Network Learning with Evolutionary Strategies for Structure Discovery
abstract: Discovering the underlying structure of Bayesian networks from data is a significant challenge in machine learning and knowledge representation. This research presents a novel approach utilizing evolutionary strategies to efficiently explore the vast space of possible network topologies. The proposed method dynamically adapts the search process, evaluating candidate network structures based on their predictive accuracy and computational complexity. Specifically, we employ an evolutionary algorithm to iteratively refine a Bayesian network structure, optimizing for both accuracy in modeling the observed data and efficiency in terms of both time and memory. The core innovation lies in the integration of Bayesian network learning with evolutionary optimization, creating a powerful tool for discovering complex and potentially intricate network structures directly from data. The resulting network structure is formally represented as (G = (V, E), P), where V is the set of nodes (variables), E is the set of edges representing dependencies, and P is the conditional probability distribution function. The evolutionary strategy is defined by a population of networks, each represented by its structure (E) and associated parameters (P). The fitness function F(G) quantifies the quality of a network, typically measured as the log-likelihood of the observed data given the network structure and parameters. The algorithm iteratively applies selection, mutation, and crossover operators to evolve the population towards higher fitness. The optimization process can be expressed mathematically as: arg minG ∈ Population F(G) = ∑i=1N log P(xi | G) where N is the number of data instances, and xi represents the observed data for the i-th instance. The evolution is guided by the selection pressure favoring networks with higher log-likelihood, and the mutation introduces structural variations (adding/removing edges) and parameter adjustments. The success of the approach is evaluated using metrics such as the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to balance model complexity and goodness-of-fit.

title: Broad Quantum Error Correction Algorithm Validation via Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum computing to validate the performance and robustness of quantum error correction (QEC) codes. The core claim is the development of a novel QEC algorithm designed to efficiently simulate and analyze QEC systems, ultimately enhancing their fidelity and resilience to errors. We explore the potential of quantum computation to significantly accelerate the verification process compared to classical methods. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, quantum simulation techniques, and expected benefits in demonstrating the effectiveness of QEC. title: Geometric Topology for Neural Network Regularization
abstract: Geometric Topology for Neural Network Regularization explores a novel approach to neural network regularization, utilizing the principles of geometric topology to establish constraints on the network's structure. This research proposes a framework where regularization is embedded within the network's topology itself, leading to more stable and well-structured networks than traditional gradient-based methods. The core mechanism centers around defining regularization terms as geometric properties, encouraging the formation of inherent patterns and avoiding abrupt changes in the network's topology. This approach offers the potential to improve generalization performance and robustness, particularly in deep neural networks. The paper details the theoretical foundations, proposes a concrete implementation, and presents initial results demonstrating the effectiveness of this geometric topology-based regularization.
